title: The 10 states set to build the least housing relative to population growth
summary: UNLV housing research flags Nevada and North Dakota for permitting fewer homes than projected households, risking higher prices.
content: North Dakota and Nevada were the only states permitting fewer than one housing unit for every projected new household. ROBYN BECK/AFP via Getty Images North Dakota and Nevada lag badly on permits, trailing projected new household growth UNLV Lied Center report finds US permits outpace demand, but some states risk affordability Nevada construction defect law deters condos and multifamily homes, shrinking affordable supply Some states are falling behind on housing — and two are set to build fewer homes than the projected number of new households. Nationally, states are permitting an average of 1.7 homes for every projected new household — about 121,000 homes a month, compared with 72,000 projected new households, according to an October research report from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Yet, a few states are lagging behind, and they could face affordability concerns with supply falling short of future demand and pushing prices up. "The states that aren't doing well are the states that have other issues working against them," said Nicholas Irwin, coauthor of the report and research director at the Lied Center for Real Estate. This could be due to a lack of building incentives, high construction costs, and limited land availability in those states. Here are the states with the largest shortfalls between monthly permit pace and projected household growth across the US. North Dakota and Nevada are the only two states in the US that have fewer than 1 permitted unit per projected household. North Dakota is 45 permits short of its projected new households a month, and Nevada is 122 permits short of its projected new households a month. In the report's overall housing supply pipeline rankings, North Dakota ranked 48th nationally, indicating struggles across the board and poor performance on four metrics, including the building permit rate per projected household. The number of units permitted per resident in North Dakota is already 30% lower than the national average, and its number of permits issued per cost-burdened household is 12% lower than the national average. Second-to-last was Nevada. As in North Dakota, there is less permitted new housing than the number of projected new households from October 2026 to December 2027. Irwin said there are a few reasons Nevada faces this issue, one of which is state policy that disincentivizes construction. For example, in Nevada , the Construction Defect Law allows builders to be held liable for construction defects for up to 10 years after the project is completed. The law disincentivizes developers from building condos and multifamily homes, where there is more room for construction defects to affect multiple buyers and prompt lawsuits — pushing developers toward building single-family homes and away from affordable housing options, Irwin said. "Everyone responds to incentives, and developers are no different," he said. Lower approval of building permits per projected households will directly impact states already experiencing affordability concerns, which often need more housing. "The issue is for the states that already have affordability issues; they need to build well above that pace," Irwin said. "They need to be building, for every one anticipated household, they're building two housing units. That will start to put more downward pressure on prices in the future because you're starting to bend that supply curve." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Aaron Rodgers just gave a masterclass in how not to quit your job
summary: Aaron Rodgers blasted his Steelers coach and was released hours later. Career experts say his messy exit is a lesson in how not to quit a job.
content: Aaron Rodgers was released by the Pittsburgh Steelers after a fiery interview the day before Thanksgiving. Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Aaron Rodgers' exit this week became a very public workplace blowup. Career experts explain how to quit a job without burning bridges. Most workers should leave with a plan, gratitude, and a clear next step. Aaron Rodgers has given workers everywhere a masterclass in how not to quit a job . Unless, perhaps, you're a four-time NFL MVP with more than $400 million in career earnings. On Wednesday, Rodgers went on "The Pat McAfee Show" after the Pittsburgh Steelers benched him and proceeded to torch head coach Mike McCarthy. The two have a long history: They spent 13 seasons together in Green Bay and won a Super Bowl in 2011. McCarthy is now in his first season as the Steelers' coach. Rodgers said McCarthy had missed meetings, fallen asleep during others, and accidentally ended a halftime huddle during Sunday's loss to the Eagles with: "One, two, three — Packers!" It was a stunning interview that The Athletic likened to an attempted "coup." The Steelers released the 42-year-old quarterback hours later. He is now a free agent. Rodger's dramatic exit is not exactly a model for how to leave a job . As Business Insider's Tim Paradis reported in 2025 , quitting the right way typically requires separating your emotions from your actions. Alan Stein, the CEO of career-coaching firm Kadima Careers, told BI that this is advice he had to learn himself, having held 31 jobs and given notice dozens of times. "Disassociate your emotions from your actions," he said, pointing out that a former boss could become a future client, colleague, reference, or hiring manager. Blowing up relationships on the way out can follow you longer than a bad job ever will. Another rule of thumb: Resist the urge to quit on your worst day. "A lot of people run away from a bad workplace, but they have nothing to run towards," Laura Labovich, who runs an outplacement firm in the Washington, DC, area, told BI. Instead, she said, make a plan. Figure out what you want next, prepare financially if you can, and leave deliberately rather than reactively. Jim Detert, a professor at the University of Virginia's Darden School of Business, told BI that it’s smart to show gratitude, give credit, and explain that you’re leaving to pursue a role better aligned with your goals. He also advises against throwing bombs in an exit interview : If leadership wasn't listening before you said you were leaving, chances are they won't change their minds after you're gone. Of course, there are times when speaking up can be appropriate. Detert has studied the impact of speaking out for years, and suggests asking two questions before doing so: Is it safe? And is it worthwhile? Rodgers' answer was apparently "Yes." To be fair, his circumstances are unusual. Rodgers has a financial cushion most workers do not. Counting his full 2026 contract, his career earnings stand at about $418 million. That kind of security changes the calculus. For nearly everyone else, the safer play is to leave with a plan, a measured message, and as few burned bridges as possible. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: The fastest-growing opportunity for creators might be something their followers never see
summary: A Madison & Wall report shows advertisers are shifting creator economy budgets to assets as influencers become the new creative agencies
content: Advertisers are increasingly treating creators as creative agencies. Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images The fastest-growing opportunity for creators is selling advertisers their content, rather than access to their audiences. Advertisers are turning to creators as an alternative to creative agencies. The largest bucket of creator-related spending goes to platforms like Meta and YouTube to boost content, though. The fastest-growing opportunity for creators might be something their followers never see. A new report from the consultancy Madison & Wall examined how advertisers are spending on creators , breaking it down into five categories. The analysts found that the category seeing the most growth was advertisers paying for creators' assets rather than for access to their followers. "Every CMO, one of their top KPIs is 'make your spend more efficient,'" said Luke Stillman, managing director of Madison & Wall, using the acronym for key performance indicators. "Marketers say, 'We want to make creative; creators do it a lot more cheaply than our creative agencies might.'" Madison & Wall estimates that advertiser spending on creators will total $116 billion globally in 2026. Spending on creators' assets will make up $14 billion this year and nearly double to $25 billion by 2030, the report projects. The largest spending category for advertisers was "media," at $52 billion, referring to money spent to boost creators' content on platforms like Meta and YouTube . Social platforms have generally made it harder for pieces of sponsored content to organically reach creators' followers. That category is projected to grow, but not as fast as asset spending. Joe Perello, CEO of Props, a performance-based creator marketing agency, previously told Business Insider that the formula of brands paying influencers for endorsements worked until platforms began to choke off organic reach for sponsored content. "That was the beginning of the erosion of finding influencers based on their followers," he said. Marketers are turning to creators for variety and efficiency The growth in asset spending reflects a simple reality: Marketers are trying to cut costs wherever they can. Treating creators like agencies and spending to boost their content's visibility are two of the fastest and most efficient ways to do that. Imogen Coles, head of influence at WPP EMEA, said she can commission creators to make significantly more — and more varied — content than she'd get from a traditional shoot. "Even if the content isn't being posted by creators, I think the creator-first ad mentality is really valuable right now," said RJ Larese, US president of the talent agency Sixteenth. "It feels more authentic and less like an old-school ad." Madison & Wall's Stillman said creators' ability to do everything from production to live events makes them more valuable to brands. That means that even if platforms continue to squeeze organic reach, creators' slice of the pie can still grow. Brandon Lentino, chief creative officer at Viral Nation, said the growth in spending toward boosting content and buying creative assets benefits small-scale creators . Brands don't necessarily need creators with big followings if the content won't reach their audience anyway. The shift requires creators to be educated about how their content will be used so they can negotiate accordingly, Lentino added. If a creator's content is going on a billboard or in a store, it'll be worth more. Coles said she'll be watching to see if the shift leads to more standardization of asset fees, making pricing negotiations easier. She also predicted that usage rights would be the next big battleground as brands look to use AI to adapt and scale content. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: The AI apocalypse believers putting their money where their fears are
summary: AI safety experts shared how they're rethinking retirement, savings, and investments as they fear AI could wipe out humanity in the next decades.
content: AI safety experts shared how their fears of AI-driven human extinction are reshaping their money habits. CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images AI safety researchers shared how their fears of an AI catastrophe are influencing their finances. Some are saving more and investing in AI infrastructure, while others are changing how they live. Despite their warnings, some still plan financially for a future they fear may never arrive. As AI leaders have renewed warnings about the technology's potential dangers , some researchers are confronting a deeply personal question: How do you plan financially for a future you fear may never arrive? Business Insider spoke with six AI safety experts about how likely they believe an AI-driven catastrophe or human extinction is, and whether those fears have changed how they spend, save, invest, or plan for retirement. Their views don't necessarily reflect those of the wider AI research community, and their financial decisions aren't necessarily a model for others to follow. In January, seven personal finance and AI experts told Business Insider that people should continue saving for retirement, even if AI radically transforms the economy. Here's how six AI safety experts we spoke with are approaching their own financial futures. Roman Yampolskiy, computer science professor at the University of Louisville Roman Yampolskiy. Courtesy of Roman Yampolskiy Roman Yampolskiy , an AI researcher and computer science professor at the University of Louisville, estimates a 99.9% probability of human extinction from advanced AI over the next century unless humanity fundamentally changes course. But he continues to save for retirement, reasoning that even a slim chance of survival makes financial security worthwhile. "Even a 99.9% probability of extinction leaves a 0.1% chance of survival, and I would prefer not to be poor in that scenario," he told Business Insider. Yampolskiy said he's financially comfortable enough to maximize his retirement contributions while buying what he wants, partly because he avoids luxury purchases and lives in relatively affordable Kentucky. However, he said he "explicitly" avoids investing directly in labs developing advanced AI. Adam Gleave, CEO of AI alignment research nonprofit FAR.AI Adam Gleave. Courtesy of Adam Gleave Adam Gleave, CEO of AI alignment research nonprofit FAR.AI, estimates a 15% chance of an AI-driven catastrophe or human extinction over the next several decades, including a 5% chance within the next few years. Unlike researchers who have stopped saving for retirement, Gleave said he's actually saving more because he believes superintelligent AI could eliminate jobs and make his future earnings less certain. His investments are also tilted toward AI computing infrastructure, including semiconductor suppliers and computing providers. Screenshots of his holdings shared with Business Insider last month showed positions in neoclouds, including CoreWeave, and Nebius, high-bandwidth memory manufacturers like Micron, SK Hynix, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF. Gleave said roughly half his investments remain in broad-based global equity indexes for diversification, while his AI-focused holdings serve partly as a hedge against rapid technological change. "If I'm wrong and AI isn't a big deal, I'll lose on my investments, but I'll have many years of labor income to earn that loss back," he said. David Krueger, executive director of AI safety nonprofit Evitable David Krueger. Courtesy of David Krueger David Krueger , executive director of AI safety nonprofit Evitable, estimates that humanity faces a greater than 50% chance of extinction from AI, potentially within the next five years. He said humanity could lose control of advanced AI as soon as this year or next, and that those fears have profoundly shaped his personal and professional decisions. "I've dedicated my life to this cause and passed up massive financial incentives to work at AI companies," he told Business Insider. Krueger said he has also chosen not to have children and is "definitely not spending time thinking about retirement." Zvi Mowshowitz, founder of the policy nonprofit Balsa Research Zvi Mowshowitz. Courtesy of Zvi Mowshowitz Zvi Mowshowitz, an AI analyst and founder of the policy nonprofit Balsa Research, estimates a roughly 70% chance of an AI-driven catastrophe or extinction within his natural lifetime, with most of that risk concentrated over the next two to 20 years. Despite those fears, he said he continues to plan for retirement much as he otherwise would, partly for his own and his family's peace of mind. "I still plan for retirement mostly as I would have otherwise, because that could still happen," he told Business Insider. Mowshowitz said he has also made investments based on his expectations about AI's development, which he said have performed well, though he did not disclose specific holdings. His advice is to prepare for radically different AI futures without abandoning conventional financial planning, including for worlds that "look normal." Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute Nate Soares told BI that humanity only gets "one try" at aligning superintelligence — and failure would be final. Courtesy of Nate Soares Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, says there's a greater than 50% chance AI will cause human extinction within the next 10 years. His fears have shaped his retirement planning : "I do not save for retirement right now," he told The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson in an interview in October. "I have a 401(k) from when I worked at Google, but I haven't contributed for a decade," said Soares, coauthor of "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies." He believes sufficiently advanced AI could develop goals that conflict with humanity's interests and eventually become self-sufficient, potentially making the planet uninhabitable for humans. Despite his grim outlook, Soares said he remains hopeful humanity can prevent that outcome: "I don't think it's inevitable." Andreas Kirsch, former research scientist at Google DeepMind Andreas Kirsch, a former research scientist at Google DeepMind, says an AI-driven catastrophe on the scale of the COVID-19 pandemic is "quite likely within the next 5 years" if governments and AI companies fail to take sufficient precautions. He said human extinction is also possible, but remains optimistic that those outcomes can be avoided through stronger regulation, monitoring, and government intervention. "I'm an optimist if we listen to the pessimists," Kirsch told Business Insider. Despite his concerns, Kirsch said he remains conservative in his investments and hasn't changed his financial plans because of worries about extinction risks. He said he understands why some researchers, including Soares, have abandoned retirement planning, but wouldn't endorse that approach "given the high uncertainty around the outcomes and our ability to still shape them." title: Ariana Grande's public image has become a problem. 3 PR pros explain how she can fix it.
summary: Ariana Grande is promoting her new movie "Focker-In-Law" and just announced a tour documentary. It's muddling her public image, PR experts say.
content: Ariana Grande attends the London premiere of "Focker-In-Law" on November 18, 2026. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Ariana Grande has been out and about promoting her new movie "Focker-In-Law," out Friday. Months earlier, Grande's team said she was planning to "step back from visibility." Grande's PR strategy is "scattered" and lacks a coherent throughline, PR pros say. The old Hollywood cliché is that "all press is good press." Ariana Grande seems on a mission to prove the opposite. A quick scan of Grande's recent headlines outlines a rocky year for the 33-year-old singer and actor. In June, news broke that Grande and her boyfriend Ethan Slater had split, three years after the "Wicked" costars first drew attention and plenty of criticism for their romance (including from Slater's ex-wife, Lily Jay ). Around the same time, Grande kicked off her much-anticipated arena tour to support her 2024 album "Eternal Sunshine," which, in a strange choice, overlapped with the rollout of her latest album, "Petal." Released in July, the new album performed well on the charts, but reviews were mixed, with some critics describing the music as "pussyfooted" and "frustratingly vague." Throughout the summer, Grande's performances and music video premieres were overtaken by rampant speculation about her health , culminating in a spiky public statement from her team in August: "She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny," it read in part. Less than three months after leaving the stage, however, Grande is back in the press, appearing on red carpets and late-night TV shows to promote her new movie, "Focker-In-Law." Although People reported in September that Grande would remain "committed" to her promo obligations for the movie despite her planned break from the public eye, the rapid turnaround makes for an untidy narrative. "She's always in the news for the wrong reasons," Larry Kopp, a longtime PR professional and founder of The TASC Group, told Business Insider. "All press is not good press when you're talking about someone like Ariana Grande." In the upper echelon of celebrity where Grande resides, publicity is all but guaranteed; the challenge is in diligently curating it. Each public appearance will attract attention to how she looks, who she's with, and where she's going, while each misstep will be magnified. If the story can't always be all positive, it should at least be coherent. This is where Grande and her team have floundered in recent years. For such a beloved and multi-talented celebrity, Grande has displayed remarkably weak ownership of her image, PR pros agreed. Representatives for Grande did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. "Where Taylor Swift and Beyoncé are so intentional in every single step that they take, Ariana Grande feels scattered," said Mike Fahey, the founder and CEO of the PR agency Fahey Communications. "One day she's Glinda, the next day she's putting out a new album," Fahey continued, referring to Grande's role in the recent "Wicked" films , for which she was Oscar-nominated and then Oscar-snubbed in consecutive years. "Personally, even as a pop culture consumer, I have been very confused by the cadence." Although Grande is both a gifted singer and a comedic actor, Fahey said her versatility is obscured by a slapdash combination of aesthetics, personas, and public missives: "There doesn't seem to be any overarching strategy." Grande has a knack for needlessly making the news Ariana Grande performs during the Eternal Sunshine Tour in London. Julian Dakdouk As the first "Wicked" film proved , Grande's comedic chops are some of her most valuable skills, celebrated by fans and critics alike. And many critics are praising Grande's scene-stealing turn in "Focker-In-Law," in which she plays a discerning former FBI hostage negotiator and foil to Ben Stiller's bumbling, well-meaning everyman. With savvier navigation of the PR machine, Grande's return to the limelight could have been tallied cleanly as a triumph, a highlight on her résumé. Instead, the statement released by Grande's team in August laid the groundwork for a visible flip-flop — a dangerous game to play when all comments and actions are thoroughly documented and analyzed online. "In 2026, in the social media era, contradictions are hypocrisy," Fahey said. Announcing that Grande would be "taking a step back from visibility" was ill-advised and ill-timed, Kopp and Fahey said. It added fuel to the speculative fire surrounding her well-being, when a simpler solution was obvious: let the embers simmer down naturally. After playing 41 sold-out shows, most fans would have expected Grande to take a break anyway, and she could have done so without a formal announcement. "Good publicists understand that less is more," Kopp said. "When a PR team comments, they're creating a story. They're putting scaffolding on the story. They're building it up." Kayley Cornelius, a celebrity PR specialist at Press Box PR, agreed that Grande's statement left too much open to interpretation. "Her team may have felt that gave her room to finish the work she wanted to do and then take a break," Cornelius said via email. "But if you're a fan reading that statement, you could quite reasonably take it to mean you won't be seeing her for a while. That makes the next time she does appear a story in itself." This isn't the first time Grande has seemed to contradict herself in public. In 2024, Grande announced plans to scale back her pop-star career to focus on musical theater; the "Eternal Sunshine" deluxe edition arrived less than five months later, followed closely by the Eternal Sunshine Tour and then another brand-new pop album. Grande also dropped out of the West End revival of "Sunday in the Park with George," scheduled to open in London next summer. On Tuesday, in the midst of "Focker-In-Law" release week, Grande announced a tour documentary, "The Eternal Sunshine Diaries," and a new concert film. "She has no throughline," Kopp said. "A good business manager, a good publicist, a good lawyer, good people around her should be giving her good advice, and it doesn't seem like they're giving it to her. Or they're giving it to her, and she's not listening." A real break could help refresh Grande's image Ariana Grande attends the New York City premiere of "Focker-In-Law." Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Universal Pictures Grande has been famous since she was a tween on Nickelodeon, but ever since 2018, when she dominated headlines with her whirlwind engagement to Pete Davidson and her smash-hit breakup anthem "Thank U, Next," Grande has been an obsessive fixture of tabloid coverage and social media snark. "One of the recurring themes in Ariana's media coverage has been how often the conversation around her personal life carries over into her work," Cornelius said. "Even when she's had major career moments, particularly with 'Wicked,' the headlines haven't always been about her performances." It's a vicious cycle that repeats every time Grande steps out with a new hairstyle, a new boyfriend, or yet another new song about the haters . "Is it really my fault you all gave me your hearts of your own accord? I don't really think so," Grande sings in her latest No. 1 hit , "Hate That I Made You Love Me." She may be right, and the harsh, competitive fame game is the true culprit here. Contradictory statements and overlapping projects are nickels and dimes in the grand scheme of public interest. At the same time, Grande is a multimillion-dollar brand, and if she wants to keep it that way, she isn't exempt from playing along. "Her movies are blockbuster smashes," Fahey said. "You can't say it's the public's fault when the public has built you into the celebrity that you are today." "I would tell her to take an actual break, actually get better, heal whatever it is that's haunting her right now," Fahey continued. The cycle is plenty fed, and an earnest reprieve from scrutiny could give her team the time and space to reset her reputation — and Grande the time she may need to refine her vision as an artist, then return with a project imbued with passion and meaning, something that will stand the test of time. "No more personal life in the news, no more chicanery, no more drama. Just stay out of the news as best you can for a while," Kopp said. "The great thing about someone like Ariana is that her art, her music, is still there. It doesn't go away." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: A new round was supposed to give US tanks more firepower. The Army is still waiting for most of them.
summary: The Army received just 180 of nearly 12,000 new tank rounds due by July, as production problems delayed the ammunition for years.
content: An Army tank crew fires a M1A2 Abrams tank during Table IV training at Fort Hood, Texas, Sept. 20, 2026. Spc. Nathan StarrUS Army The Army received just 180 of nearly 12,000 rounds of a new tank ammunition due by July. Production problems have delayed the new multipurpose ammunition for years. Despite delays, the Army has already ordered 10,000 more rounds from manufacturer Northrop Grumman. The US Army has received just 180 of nearly 12,000 new tank rounds that were scheduled for delivery by this summer, as production problems delayed ammunition meant to give Abrams crews more flexibility in combat, a Pentagon watchdog has found. The new 120mm Advanced Multi-Purpose round is designed to replace the capabilities of several types of older ammunition for Army tanks . The new round can be used against more targets, including anti-tank missile teams and reinforced concrete walls, and alleviates crews from having to carry different rounds for other uses. But the Army only accepted its first rounds in December 2024, over three years after deliveries were originally due, according to a recently released Defense Department inspector general report . As of late July, the contractor, which was not named in the report but has previously been identified as Northrop Grumman, had delivered just 180 of the nearly 12,000 rounds scheduled for delivery by that time, the report said. The Army has contracted for nearly 22,000 rounds in total, including rounds beyond those scheduled for delivery by the July cutoff. "The M1147 AMP is a critical capability for our warfighters and we remain committed to the program's success," Northrop Grumman told Business Insider. "We will continue to support the US Army as we work together to deliver this important capability." The contractor encountered technical and production problems that contributed to years of delays, the report said. Among them was leaking primer material found during testing in 2025. The company paused production involving those parts and did not deliver rounds with leaking primers, the watchdog said. Despite the delays, the Army awarded Northrop another contract this March for 10,000 more rounds. Officials told inspectors that switching contractors wouldn't be practical because the company had already made progress developing the ammunition , despite believing that choosing another company might have reduced production risks. The Army's assessment reports rated the contractor's performance as "marginal" or "unsatisfactory" in five of seven reviews since 2018, the watchdog found. Army officials said changes to improve performance could add costs, and potentially relieve the contractor of responsibility for its work. Because of delays and technical challenges, the Pentagon may not even receive the full value from the nearly $224 million that has been obligated for the contract for over a decade, the report said. The delays come as the Pentagon faces broader concerns about whether US manufacturers can produce enough ammunition for a major conflict. In a separate report released this month, the Government Accountability Office said the military has faced persistent munitions shortages , exacerbated by the war in Iran , and lacks plans linking production and funding to military requirements. "DOD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement," that previous report said. title: Ben Stiller's 10 best and 10 worst movies, according to critics
summary: Ben Stiller has a lot of hits among his best movies, like "Tropic Thunder" and "The Royal Tenenbaums," but he also has plenty of duds.
content: Ben Stiller. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images These are the best and worst movies of Ben Stiller's 40-year career. Critics loved some of his comedy classics and dramatic works. Three of Stiller's movies have a 0% score on Rotten Tomatoes. From raunchy comedies to stirring dramatic performances, Ben Stiller has been in every kind of movie imaginable. Best known for his comedic talents in memorable movies like "There's Something About Mary" and "Meet the Parents" (the latest movie in that franchise, "Focker-In-Law," is in theaters now), Stiller has also delivered more serious performances in movies like "Greenberg" and "Flirting with Disaster." But, being in the business for four decades, there are going to be some duds from time to time, and Stiller has a few of those, including three movies that have the dreaded 0% score on Rotten Tomatoes. Below are Ben Stiller's 10 best and 10 worst movies, according to Rotten Tomatoes. Note: This list does not include documentaries. All scores were current on the date of publication and are subject to change. Here are the best movies of Ben Stiller's career. Ben Stiller. Tiziana Fabi/AFP/Getty Images 10. Stiller played a guy stuck in a rut in "Greenberg," which was a critical darling in 2010. "Greenberg." Focus Features. Rotten Tomatoes score: 76% From writer-director Noah Baumbach, Stiller plays Roger Greenberg, who, after being released from a psychiatric hospital after a nervous breakdown, is now doing nothing in Los Angeles. He connects with Florence (Greta Gerwig), who brings meaning to his life. 9. Stiller voiced Alex the lion in "Madagascar 3: Europe's Most Wanted" (2012), from the hit animated franchise. "Madagascar 3: Europe's Most Wanted." DreamWorks Animation Rotten Tomatoes score: 77% Stiller plays a lion from the Central Park Zoo who, along with other animals from the zoo, tries to get back to New York City by traveling through Europe with a circus. 8. In the drama "Brad's Status" (2017), Stiller played a father taking his son to tour colleges. "Brad's Status." Amazon Studios Rotten Tomatoes score: 78% Before creating the "White Lotus" series, Mike White wrote and directed this dramedy starring Stiller as a father who is determined to make sure his son doesn't make the mistakes he did. 7. In 2001, Stiller was part of the ensemble cast of Wes Anderson's acclaimed movie, "The Royal Tenenbaums." "The Royal Tenenbaums." Buena Vista Pictures Rotten Tomatoes score: 81% This Wes Anderson classic was beloved by the critics when it came out. Stiller starred alongside Gene Hackman, Anjelica Huston, Bill Murray, Gwyneth Paltrow, Owen Wilson, and Luke Wilson . Stiller plays one of three gifted Tenenbaum siblings who, after finding great success in their youth, find disappointment in adulthood. 6. Stiller directed and starred in 2008's "Tropic Thunder," which has become a comedy classic. "Tropic Thunder." DreamWorks Pictures Rotten Tomatoes score: 82% From Robert Downey Jr. in blackface to an unrecognizable Tom Cruise as a despicable studio head, Stiller is at the top of his comedic game in "Tropic Thunder," which he directed and starred in. The movie follows Hollywood star Tugg Speedman (Stiller), who, after a string of box office busts, hopes starring in a war movie will put him back on top. 5. "There's Something About Mary" (1998) made Stiller the go-to comedy actor of the 1990s. "There's Something About Mary." 20th Century Fox Rotten Tomatoes score: 84% This Farrelly brothers gross-out comedy was beloved by both the critics and audiences. Stiller plays Ted Stroehmann, a guy who still thinks about his high school crush, Mary (Cameron Diaz). The problem is, so does everyone else who lays eyes on her. 4. Stiller copes with getting older by hanging out with millennials in "While We're Young" (2014). "While We're Young." A24 Rotten Tomatoes score: 84% Noah Baumbach enters the list again. This time, he cast Stiller and Naomi Watts as a couple whose relationship is tested after they befriend a couple in their 20s played by Adam Driver and Amanda Seyfried. 3. Critics consider "Meet the Parents" (2000) to be Stiller's greatest comedic work. "Meet the Parents." Universal Pictures Rotten Tomatoes score: 85% Critics and audiences alike were shocked to see Stiller team with Robert De Niro. But all are happy it happened. Now considered a comedy classic, Stiller plays Greg Focker, who wants to propose to his girlfriend (Teri Polo) but wants to get the permission of her father (De Niro) first. What transpires is a series of hilarious, unfortunate events that make it even harder for Greg to connect. 2. Stiller played a man searching for his biological parents in "Flirting with Disaster" (1996). "Flirting with Disaster." Miramax Films Rotten Tomatoes score: 88% In this indie movie from David O. Russell, Stiller plays a new father who sets out to find his biological parents. It turns into a road trip that makes him question everything, including his relationship with his wife (Patricia Arquette). 1.
