title: Elon Musk upped the ante on his SpaceX share Trump Account giveaway
summary: Elon Musk said he would gift a SpaceX share to every American child every year, on top of one share each from the company.
content: Donald Trump and Elon Musk. Bloomberg/Getty Images Elon Musk said the night before Thanksgiving that every American child will get two SpaceX shares. Less than 24 hours afterward, he upped that to one share every year. "Vital that children have a stake in the future," he said in an X post. Less than 24 hours after announcing plans to give SpaceX shares to every child in the US, Elon Musk upped the ante in his Trump account giveaway. He said on Thursday that he would gift a SpaceX share to every American child every year. "Vital that children have a stake in the future," Musk added in a post on X. It comes after Musk said Wednesday that every child would get two SpaceX shares: one from the company, and one from himself. He had first promised in October to give a share to every child. Musk said that the shares from SpaceX will be transferred next month, and his will be transferred when his lockup expires in June. SpaceX's share price opened around $130 on Friday. Based on 2025 census data, there are roughly 72 million children in the US. So, if Musk gifted 72 million shares right now, they would be worth around $9.4 billion. Given his latest pledge, a child could receive 19 shares over 18 years — one from SpaceX and up to 18 from Musk. At the current share price, those would be worth nearly $2,500. The value could rise or fall depending on SpaceX's performance, but Musk has lofty ambitions. On Thursday, he said that if SpaceX succeeded in making life multiplanetary and harnessing a millionth of the sun's energy, it could be worth about a million times the current global economy — a figure equivalent to roughly $128 quintillion , based on International Monetary Fund estimates. He acknowledged those were "absurdly difficult goals," but added: "I recommend holding on to your shares." It appears likely the shares will be transferred to Trump Accounts. The Trump administration launched the initiative this summer, with those born between 2025 and 2028 receiving a $1,000 federal seed deposit. Several companies have agreed to contribute to them as well. Michael and Susan Dell contributed $250 to 25 million Trump Accounts last month. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband also pledged in July to give away 2 million SpaceX shares. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I ranked every custard shake at Shake Shack from worst to best, including its 3 holiday flavors
summary: Shake Shack introduced three limited-edition flavors in November. I compared them to the chain's other custard shakes, and only one really impressed me.
content: The holiday shakes from Shake Shack this year. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Shake Shack released three special shakes for the holiday season. I tried them to see how they compared to other Shake Shack shakes. I thought two of the new flavors were OK, but I really enjoyed one. Over the past couple of years, I've embarked on a grueling mission: to taste and rank every shake on Shake Shack 's menu. Shake Shack has seven main milkshake flavors available year-round, plus three or four limited-edition flavors at any given time. The latest additions to the menu are the Christmas Cookie shake, the Butterscotch Crème Brûlée shake, and the Hazelnut Chocolate shake. I tried these to see how they compared to other Shake Shack flavors — in total, I've tried 19 of the shakes, each made with frozen custard. The flavors include classics such as chocolate and vanilla, as well as limited-edition shakes like the Dubai Chocolate Pistachio, which was introduced last summer and brought back this year due to popular demand. Here's how I ranked them all, from my least favorite to my favorite. Shake Shack did not respond to a request for comment. In last place came the strawberry shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider A strawberry shake costs $6 at my nearest Shake Shack in New York. It's made with vanilla custard and "real strawberry," according to the website. There are 690 calories in a 16-ounce cup, Shake Shack's standard shake size. It was doomed from the start — I almost couldn't get past its strong strawberry fumes. Inside the strawberry shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This could just be personal bias, as I would never order a strawberry shake under any circumstances, but when I took the lid off and sniffed the shake, I felt like I was sniffing a strawberry-scented candle. After tasting a sip, I was able to appreciate that this was one of the thickest shakes I tried. But it was just too sweet for me — I could only take a couple sips before feeling like I was rapidly developing a cavity. In 18th place was the limited-edition Campfire S'mores shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The Campfire S'mores shake, which was available during summer 2025, was made with vanilla frozen custard, graham crackers, "chocolate and toasted marshmallow fudge chunks," and finished off with whipped cream and s'mores crumbles, per Shake Shack's website description. It cost $6.99 and had 1,090 calories. You can see how many of the ingredients were sitting at the bottom, making this hard to drink. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider There sure was a lot in there, but to me, this just tasted like a vanilla shake with some graham cracker bits mixed in, which was pretty unpleasant, texturally speaking. I couldn't taste chocolate or marshmallows, two of the three key s'mores ingredients. In my opinion, it was not worth the extra 50 cents or the extra calories. This year's s'mores offering, the Chocolate Toasted Marshmallow S'mores shake, was a slight improvement. Chocolate Toasted Marshmallow S'mores Shake Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This summer, instead of focusing on s'mores, the shake is more marshmallow-forward, which I really only got from the whipped cream. This shake contains vanilla custard with a toasted marshmallow dark chocolate ganache, and is topped with whipped cream and a s'mores graham cracker crunch, which turned out to be crumbled graham crackers and little chocolate crumbles. It costs $7.69 and has 1,110 calories. This was more chocolate-forward than last year's marshmallow shake, but I still didn't love it. Chocolate Toasted Marshmallow S'mores Shake Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I shouldn't have complained about not tasting the marshmallow last summer, because the first sip I took off the top was like drinking a liquified marshmallow, with some graham cracker thrown in. Once I tasted the actual shake, though, I thought it seemed more like a black-and-white shake than a vanilla one, which was one of my issues last year. However, this still isn't for me. Maybe I just don't want to combine s'mores and shakes? At No. 16 was another limited-edition shake: the Dubai Chocolate Pistachio shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Nobody is immune to Dubai chocolate, not even Shake Shack. Shake Shack's version of the viral snack — a chocolate bar filled with green pistachio cream and shredded phyllo pastry — is a shake that costs $10.99 and has 1,330 calories. It's made with pistachio custard mixed with "toasted kataifi shredded phyllo" and is topped with mashed-up pistachios and kataifi. It's encased in a crackable shell made of dark chocolate inside the cup, so it makes sense that Shake Shack recommends that it's best enjoyed cold. I barely tasted any chocolate, and the shredded phyllo made this hard to drink, as well. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider To me, this didn't taste like chocolate at all, since the chocolate was completely frozen and didn't mix with the pistachio custard. The pistachio custard itself was delicious, but the phyllo mixed in felt strange to drink … almost as if paper had been added to my shake. Since this was a more expensive shake, I can't rank it any higher. But Shake Shack should definitely add a pistachio flavor to its lineup — I would drink it plain. Shake Shack didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider regarding its Dubai chocolate recipe or pricing. My least favorite holiday shake was the Christmas Cookie shake. The Christmas Cookie shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I visited Shake Shack's Innovation Kitchen in December 2025 to try out the new holiday flavors, so I didn't pay for this one, but according the chain's website, it retailed at $6.99 and had 840 calories. I tried it again this year and had the same reaction. It was made with sugar-cookie custard and topped with whipped cream and red and green sprinkles. Apparently, this is a fan favorite, but it was too sweet for my taste. Christmas Cookie shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Nick Wuest, Shake Shack's senior manager of culinary innovation, said the Christmas Cookie shake has stayed on the menu year after year due to demand, and when Shake Shack tinkered with the recipe, fans let them know they want it left untouched. I'll give them this: It certainly tasted like a sugar cookie in shake form. However, as just a mild lover of sugar cookies, I found this too sweet, though I was impressed by how accurate the flavor was. In 14th place was the vanilla-and-chocolate shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This is exactly what it sounds like: vanilla and chocolate custard mixed together. It has 720 calories and costs $6. This tasted like chocolate with a hint of vanilla, but not in a good way. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Maybe it's because the chocolate was so overpowering compared to the vanilla, which can be more subtle, but this just tasted like a watered-down chocolate shake to me. The chocolate shake was just slightly above that at 13. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This is just frozen chocolate custard. It's $6 and 750 calories. This was a flavorful chocolate shake, but I wasn't overly impressed. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider As a chocolate ice cream lover, I thought this was sure to place high. Instead, this chocolate shake was somewhat middling for me. I thought it had an artificial aftertaste, and I couldn't take more than a couple of sips, something that never happens to me with chocolate ice cream. But some chocolate is better than no chocolate, hence its spot at No. 13. Next, the limited-edition Banana Pudding shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The Banana Pudding shake, another limited-time shake that was on the menu until the end of summer 2025, used banana custard made with "real banana," per Shake Shack, and was mixed with vanilla wafer cookies. It was also topped with "vanilla wafer cookie crumble." It was priced at $6.99 and had 1,010 calories. It was delicious, but the smell knocked it down a few spots in the ranking. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Banana-flavored anything can be divisive — remember how mad some people would get on Halloween if they got banana Laffy Taffy ? — but I thought this was great. It tasted like real bananas, the cookie crumble on top was good, and the cookies only added flavor, rather than a crumb-like texture in the shake. Ranking a vanilla shake somewhere in the middle seems right. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The Shake Shack site writes that its vanilla shakes are made with "real vanilla" in the vanilla custard. One shake contains 680 calories and costs $6. It was the creamiest shake I tried. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This was easily the creamiest, thickest shake I tried. Can you go wrong with a vanilla shake? It's sweet, doesn't have a strong aftertaste, and was the only one that actually felt like I was quenching any type of thirst. However, it's kind of bland, as many vanilla things are. So I can't put it any higher. The second holiday shake for 2026 is the Hazelnut Chocolate shake, topped with a piece of Ferrero Rocher chocolate. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The first new shake for 2026 is this Hazelnut Chocolate shake, which is also crackable. It's a vanilla shake spun with chocolate-hazelnut spread, poured into a cup with a dark chocolate shell. It's topped with whipped cream, chopped hazelnuts, wafer flakes, and a piece of Ferrero Rocher chocolate. I tried this at the Innovation Kitchen, so I didn't pay, but it would cost $9.99. It has 1,470 calories. Much like the Dubai Chocolate shake, the dark chocolate shell didn't add much, but I liked the piece of Ferrero Rocher on top. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I know this supposedly is swirled with hazelnut, but it just tasted like a vanilla shake, which is why it's right above the vanilla shake, because I liked the extra piece of chocolate and the hazelnut crunchies on top. But fundamentally, this basically tasted like a vanilla shake. This summer's best new flavor was the Key Lime Pie shake, until recently. Key Lime Pie shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The third and final shake released earlier this summer is the Key Lime Pie shake, which is made with vanilla custard spun with Key-lime pie curd and graham cracker crunch. It's then topped with whipped cream and more graham crackers. It's $7.69 and 1,020 calories. This would've been a perfect shake, if not for the aftertaste. Key Lime Pie shake, Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I love Key-lime pie, so I was excited to try this. Even just taking off the lid and taking an exploratory sniff, I knew that Shake Shack had done a good job. It smelled like summer. I was further rewarded when I took a sip and tasted a liquified Key-lime pie. Maybe that doesn't sound appetizing, but it was delicious. However, after taking a couple of sips, I couldn't ignore the artificial aftertaste, which prevents me from putting this any higher. I liked the crackable Peppermint Bark Chocolate shake better than the Dubai Chocolate and the Hazelnut Chocolate shakes. The Peppermint Bark Chocolate shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Another holiday offering from 2025, the Peppermint Bark Chocolate shake ($9.99, 1,320 calories) contained chocolate custard infused with mint chocolate fudge, encased in a crackable peppermint white chocolate shell. It was topped with whipped cream and little pieces of peppermint candy. This tasted like winter to me. The Peppermint Bark Chocolate shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Shake Shack's second foray into the crackable shake space was, in my opinion, an improvement on the first. It was much easier to crack and pull out pieces of the shell. My main critique of the Dubai Chocolate shake was that I didn't really taste any chocolate. Since this was a chocolate shake infused with mint fudge, there was no missing either flavor. Of course, not everyone likes mint chocolate, but if you find yourself grabbing a peppermint mocha every day of December, I'd give this a whirl next holiday season — or at least, I would've if they'd brought it back this year, but they didn't. In seventh place came the limited-edition Oreo Cookie Funnel Cake flavor. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The Oreo Cookie Funnel Cake shake, another summer 2025 option, was made with vanilla custard and "Oreo Cookies and funnel cake crunch" spun into the custard. It was topped with whipped cream and Oreo crumbles. It had 1,140 calories — the second most of all the shakes I tried — and cost $6.99. This, somehow, tasted exactly like a funnel cake you'd get at a local fair. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I was curious to see how this would taste different from the regular cookies-and-cream shake, but the two couldn't have been more different. Somehow, this just tasted exactly like a funnel cake you'd get at a carnival. It even had the sugary aftertaste, which I love: It brought me back to summer nights that I spent at my local town fair, licking powdered sugar off my fingers. If I had to knock it, though, I didn't really taste Oreo in the shake itself, though the crumbles on top somewhat made up for it. My favorite holiday offering from this year is the Butterscotch Crème Brûlée shake. Butterscotch Crème Brûlée shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This shake is butterscotch crème brûlée-flavored custard. It's topped with whipped cream and honeycomb pieces. It has 950 calories and would retail for $7.49 (I also got to try it in the test kitchen). This was very unique, and I appreciated that. Butterscotch crème brûlée shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider If you've ever been to the Wizarding World of Harry Potter at Universal Studios, this might be somewhat familiar, as I imagine this is what a Butterbeer shake would taste like. The butterscotch taste certainly comes through, and I liked the somewhat smoky flavor from the honeycomb pieces on top. Next up was the coffee shake. The coffee shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider After a five-year hiatus, the coffee shake was reintroduced to the permanent menu in September 2025, ahead of National Coffee Day. It costs $6 and has 700 calories, and is made with vanilla custard mixed with dark roast coffee. This was the platonic ideal of a coffee shake. The coffee shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider As a self-proclaimed coffee ice cream aficionado, I was a bit nervous to try this flavor. Sometimes, coffee-flavored products can taste artificial or too sweet, but I didn't have to worry about that with this shake. Simply put, this tasted like a frozen cup of coffee. If that sounds appealing to you, I'd recommend. In fourth place came the limited-edition Sticky Toffee Pudding flavor. The Sticky Toffee Pudding shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This shake, another 2025 holiday flavor, had 930 calories and cost $6.99. It's made with a vanilla custard base, a piece of sticky toffee pudding cake, and caramelized brown sugar blended together, topped with whipped cream and a toffee pudding sauce. This was delicious. The Sticky Toffee Pudding shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Of the three holiday flavors from last year, I have the least experience with sticky toffee pudding, a British dessert. I was a bit worried I wouldn't enjoy it, but my fears quickly vanished after the first sip. To me, the molasses flavoring was like a gingerbread cookie, making it the perfect holiday treat. I also liked that I could feel the little pieces of cake mixed in, adding a textural dimension that some of the other shakes didn't have. In third place: the black-and-white shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider This is vanilla custard mixed with chocolate fudge sauce. It has 770 calories and costs $6.49. This tasted like vanilla with a hint of chocolate, in a good way. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Full disclosure: Before doing this ranking, I thought that a black-and-white shake was just chocolate and vanilla mixed together. But no! It's a vanilla shake mixed with chocolate sauce. I much preferred this. It had more of a taste than a plain vanilla shake, but it didn't have the watered-down quality of the vanilla-and-chocolate shake, which was overwhelmed by chocolate. This tasted like a hot fudge sundae. I highly recommend. In second place is the Biscoff Cookie Butter Tiramisu Shake. The Biscoff Cookie Butter Tiramisu shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider In August 2026, Shake Shack debuted its latest custard creation: the Biscoff Cookie Butter Tiramisu shake. It contains tiramisu custard mixed with Biscoff cookie butter and Biscoff cookie crumbs. It's topped with whipped cream and even more of the cookie crumbs. It's 1,140 calories and costs $7.49. I downed around half of it in 5 minutes. It was worth the brain freeze. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider As a huge fan of cookie butter and tiramisu, I had high hopes I would like this shake, and my expectations were exceeded. I took a sip and actually gasped in delight. I loved the subtle hint of coffee in the tiramisu custard, and the chunks of Biscoff cookies were perfect for adding a little texture. I also enjoyed the crumbles on top, which added a mouth-watering aroma to the shake. Sometimes, even if it's a shake I enjoy, I can't drink it too fast. Not so here: This shake didn't feel too heavy, or too sweet, so I was able to take huge sips. It also paired well with fries, which I dunked in the shake for a salty/sweet combo. And in first place — certainly not to my own surprise — was the cookies-and-cream shake. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The cookies-and-cream shake ($6.49 and 850 calories) is made with vanilla custard and spun with "chocolate cookie crumbles." This was, to put it plainly, so good. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider In almost any scenario, I am ordering a cookies-and-cream shake. It's been my go-to for years … but that just means that the Shake Shack shake had to live up to my high standards. And it did. This tasted like drinking a mashed-up Oreo, which is all I ever want from a cookies-and-cream shake. It was creamy, not too sweet, and the texture of the cookie crumbles wasn't off-putting in any way. It had just the right amount of crumbs. I'd be fine with getting any of the top 10 shakes, but cookies and cream will forever be my No. 1 choice. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I flew on an African airline I'd never heard of. Here's what surprised me about the experience.
summary: ASKY Airlines, launched its first flight in 2010, and has become a solid option for pan-African travel, but it's not this writer's first choice.
content: I flew from Monrovia, Liberia, to Dakar, Senegal, on ASKY Airlines. Manseen Logan/BI I flew the pan-African airline ASKY from Monrovia, Liberia, to Dakar, Senegal. It felt like one of the smoothest and safest flights I took this year. However, the amenities were not consistent on each leg of the flight, and the food was bland. Imagine preparing to fly on an airline you've never heard of that has midlevel reviews. That was my experience earlier this month. I booked a round-trip flight on ASKY Airlines from Monrovia, Liberia, to Dakar, Senegal, to take care of some family business in Liberia before heading to Senegal for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games . I've been traveling internationally since I was 12, and I've taken a variety of flights, from economy on Frontier to business class on Japan Airlines. In all my years, I'd never heard of the pan-African Airline ASKY, but it was the fastest and most affordable option I had. So I did what any budgetnista would do: I did some research, bought the ticket, and hoped for the best. The reviews were mixed. One YouTube video from 2024 cited a dirty plane but a smooth ride. Another from 2022 mentioned mediocre food, but a comfortable flight. After trying ASKY Airlines out for myself, the overall experience was better than I expected, but it wouldn't be my go-to for traveling in Africa. The cost and route surprised me. Manseen Logan/BI I was most surprised at how expensive and difficult it is to travel within Africa . Before booking my ticket from Liberia to Senegal, which is less than 1,200 miles apart, I budgeted for a ticket from New York City to Dakar on Delta Air Lines. The US had direct flights to Dakar, but Monrovia, Liberia, which sits on the same West Coast of Africa, didn't. Every flight I looked at had multiple stops and layovers. Additionally, the price points weren't that different. You could find flights from New York to Dakar for between $800 and $1,200 depending on the dates. Flying from Liberia was very much the same. I ended up paying $1,058 for my round-trip flight with a quick stop in Accra, Ghana, and a short layover, where we switched planes in the ASKY hub, Lomé, Togo. Checking in luggage was standard. Manseen Logan/BI I was able to bring two large suitcases (up to 50 lbs each), a carry-on , and a personal item for free. I didn't have any trouble checking in my luggage or receiving it at my destination. That process was pretty standard, and I didn't have to retrieve my bags until I reached my final destination in Dakar. It was one of the smoothest flights I took this year. Manseen Logan/BI The takeoff and landing of the roughly nine-hour flight (including layovers) were smooth from start to finish. We didn't encounter any turbulence or rough winds. On the other hand, when I was flying back to the States from Monrovia on United Airlines, I was met with delays due to the FAA grounding flights and turbulence when we finally got in the air, but it was still a great flight back to the US. I had two very different experiences arriving at and departing from my destination. Manseen Logan/BI Even though I purchased the same economy ticket both ways, and the reservation listed all of the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max, I flew on very different planes throughout the flight. Going to Dakar from Lomé, the seats had soft fabric, offered more legroom, and displayed on-screen entertainment. Returning to Monrovia, the seats were different, with tighter legroom and no screens for entertainment. The experience seems to depend on the specific aircraft, not solely the ticket class. I didn't expect to fly back to Monrovia without entertainment. ASKY offered box office hits and a variety of movies for entertainment. Manseen Logan/BI I expected the airline to have a variety of movies, but I was impressed with the global box office hits, like "Sinners," that were available. The movie selection was similar to any other airline, with more African movie selections, which I expected from a pan-African airline. The food lacked the flavor I'd expect from an African airline. Manseen Logan/BI I didn't recognize any of the entrées that were provided, but I was still excited to try them. I enjoyed the papaya and watermelons, the rolls, biscuits, and couscous with salad dressing. However, the entrées tasted blander than I would've liked. Can they serve pepper sauce on a plane? On the side, at least? It was a great overall flight. Manseen Logan/BI I always enjoy boarding and deboarding a plane from the tarmac. It makes me feel like I can see where I'm going, which makes me feel a bit more secure. Throughout my flight on ASKY, I felt safe and comfortable. However, if I had the option to choose my airline, I would go with one that has a more up-to-date and consistent fleet that can offer similar experiences each way. title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback may herald an 'age of resentment,' top economist Steve Hanke says
summary: Jensen Huang return to Nvidia as CEO may fuel broader resentment toward those who appear to break the rules and get away with it, Steve Hanke said.
content: Jensen Huang was recently reinstated as Nvidia's CEO. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia may herald an "age of resentment," Steve Hanke says. The veteran economist said people feel indignant when others seem to get away with breaking the rules. Hanke said that resentment can be polarizing, pushing people further to the left and right. Jensen Huang's stunning return to Nvidia sent investors into raptures, but it has rankled many others and could have sweeping repercussions, veteran economist Steve Hanke says. "Thanks to the likes of Jensen Huang, I think that we are entering an age of resentment that promises a great many problems in the sphere of economic policy," Hanke told Business Insider. Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on November 12 following reports that he had extramarital affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a direct report. He was reinstated 11 days later, on November 23, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to bring him back. The news sent Nvidia stock up 31% on the day, adding nearly $1 trillion to the AI chipmaker's market capitalization, but it has since given up some of those gains. The conduct of Silicon Valley types like Huang "flouts the moral sentiments and rules that govern and control most people's behavior," fueling public bitterness toward "this new class of big players," Hanke said. The professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University, who served on President Ronald Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, said many onlookers are indignant because they feel they've been "treated unfairly" by comparison, and have been "slighted, or abandoned, or humiliated." In other words, they see a lack of accountability for the likes of Huang and believe they can break the rules without any lasting consequences. A big reason for the push to bring back Huang was that he's widely considered the face of AI and integral to US success in the budding sector, given Nvidia's central role in powering and financing it. But as the industry's champion, he also represents all that's wrong with AI in skeptics' eyes. Their concerns span from the safety of the tech to its impact on jobs to the immense resource demands of the data-center buildout. Steve Hanke warned of an "age of resentment." Steve Hanke Hanke warned that depth of resentment can be polarizing, spurring people on the right to embrace fascism, and those on the left to champion socialism. Indeed, Americans who felt resentful of wealthy elites helped propel Trump into power in 2016, while disillusionment with wealth inequality and political corruption has fueled the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America. "As it turns out, both the resentful on the left and the right have one thing in common: they demand that individual liberties be restricted and that the state be given more power to 'correct' things," Hanke said. Billionaire investor and economic historian Ray Dalio has been issuing similar warnings for years . "When broad-based discontent bubbles up and those in power allow it to grow, it can boil over to the point that when they try to put a lid on it, it explodes," he wrote in a LinkedIn post in 2024. Moreover, veteran investor Jeremy Grantham said in 2023 that income inequality has "resulted in the estrangement, almost bitterness and anger of at least a third of the general public who feel they have been badly treated." title: NBC is reviewing its ad process after a commercial calling for an end to US aid to Israel drew backlash
summary: Jewish advocacy groups hit out at NBC for airing IMEU's pro-Palestinian ad linking US funds to Israel's war in Gaza during an 'SNL' Thanksgiving show.
content: IMEU Policy Project/YouTube An ad for a pro-Palestine group ran during "SNL's" Thanksgiving special. Jewish advocacy groups criticized broadcaster NBC for airing the ad. NBCUniversal will evaluate its process for reviewing ads, a person said. NBCUniversal will evaluate its process for reviewing ads after it faced backlash this week over an ad from a pro-Palestinian organization that called for an end to US support for Israel. A person familiar with the matter on Friday said NBCU senior management wasn't aware of the ad until after it ran. The ad drew backlash from prominent Jewish groups and on social media. The person said the ad won't run again, but it wasn't clear if it had been slated to. Shown during a "Saturday Night Live" Thanksgiving special, the ad begins by depicting a girl who saves up $400 over the course of a year to buy a new bicycle. It then switches to a different girl who is missing one leg and standing on crutches in front of a pile of rubble, before zooming out to a scene of destroyed buildings. "Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this," the ad's narrator says. It then invites viewers to visit the campaign site NoMoreForIsrael.com. The ad, which aired on Wednesday, was placed by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, a US nonprofit organization that states its mission is to advocate for US policies that advance Palestinian rights and freedom. NBCU's decision to run the ad drew criticism from Jewish and Israel-focused advocacy groups, which argued that the 30-second spot made misleading and unsubstantiated claims about US aid and the war in Gaza. The IMEU posted on X later on Friday that it was "disheartened" to learn NBC had decided to discontinue the ad, saying it was "indisputable" and had passed the broadcaster's fact-checking requirements. 'Facts out of context' In response to the ad, the Israeli-American Council nonprofit published a petition titled "NBC, Where are your standards?" It calls on the Federal Communications Commission to investigate whether the ad complied with its rules and for NBCU to review its approval process, suspend broadcasting the ad, and publicly apologize if it was approved "without adequate factual substantiation." "We, the undersigned, express our profound disappointment and outrage at the decision of one of America's leading broadcast networks to provide a national platform for an advertisement that, in our view, takes facts out of context and uses selective information and unsubstantiated accusations to construct a misleading narrative about a complex and painful reality," the petition reads. The National Jewish Advocacy Center published a five-page letter addressed to Mark Marshall, NBCU's chairman of global advertising and partnerships, asking NBC to explain and document its decision to approve the ad. The group told Business Insider it would hand-deliver the letter to NBCU on Friday. Citing FCC rules requiring US broadcast stations to maintain public records of ads addressing political issues of national importance, the letter says an incomplete file could result in an FCC complaint. Unsupported factual claims made within the ad "may warrant reconsideration of NBC's approval and a request for corrective action," the letter says. Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the Anti-Defamation League, wrote on X that the ad was "indefensible." "At a moment of escalating antisemitism , there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative," Greenblatt said. Ted Deutch, CEO of the American Jewish Committee, wrote on X that NBC should explain how the ad met its standards. "The suffering of Palestinian civilians is real and heartbreaking," Deutch said. "But using that suffering to demonize Israel while writing Hamas out of the story isn't an honest debate." The dispute over the ad highlights the broader debate over US military assistance to Israel and over Israel's war in Gaza . In an interview with Semafor ahead of the ad's TV broadcast, an IMEU executive said the ad was created to raise awareness of reported US-Israel negotiations on a new long-term security agreement. The current 10-year military-aid Memorandum of Understanding expires in 2028, and no new agreement has been publicly confirmed. "We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going," Margaret DeReus, the IMEU's executive director, told Semafor. title: I wanted an iPod for my kids. I found this device instead.
summary: For kids too young for a phone, a music player that can do Spotify or Apple Music — and doesn't have an internet browser — is tricky.
content: The Globluum music player is slightly larger than a cassette, and great for kids and tweens. Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider Parents are looking for a music player for their kids who aren't old enough for a phone. My goal: something that can stream Spotify, Amazon, and Apple music, but doesn't have an internet browser or other apps. I recommend this $70 music player for tweens and kids! The children of today (ok, maybe their parents) yearn for an old iPod . Something I've heard over and over, both in real conversations with mom friends and in online parenting groups, is the desire to have some form of kid-friendly music player. Something like an iPod, if Apple hadn't discontinued them . I've found the solution: it's this $70 music player from Globluum . The Globluum music player for kids can offline sync Spotify, Amazon Music, and Apple Music, but has no apps or internet access. Amazon There's a new tricky age for kids when they're too old for the baby-ish Fisher Price-type versions of technology, but too young for their own phone. There are some great screen-free audio devices — the Toniebox or the Yoto player , but these are generally designed for preschoolers and young kids. The problem is with those upper-elementary and middle-school kids — let's say ages 7 to 13 — who want to listen to real adult music, not Kidz Bop or "Baby Shark." This is a crucial and formative time for kids to develop their own musical taste, and connect with peers and culture through music. If you're over 35, you probably remember buying your first CDs or cassettes at Sam Goody or Borders around this age. Maybe you even taped songs off the radio. There's a good chance that videos popular on MTV when you were 11 are still burned into your brain. But things are different now. Most people, both young and old, listen to music through a streaming app like Spotify or Apple Music, or through YouTube. And while there are good options for this at home (or hey, even a record player!), the trick is a portable player for kids when they leave the house. This was exactly my son's problem. He loved listening to music on his iPad at home, but he wanted something small he could fit in his pocket on the go. At 10, he's old enough to have his own musical taste, but too young for a phone. Here was what I was looking for in a device: No text, calling, or internet browser No games or other apps, just music Bluetooth for headphones and a built-in speaker Apple Music and Spotify compatible Can offline sync playlists so it can be played when not streaming on WiFi Doesn't need to be connected to a computer or use a cord Some form of parental controls Pocket-sized and portable I have a feeling this is the list of requirements you're looking for, too. In a twist that was shocking to me, I found that Amazon's AI assistant was actually really helpful to sort through the various options when I searched for "music player for kids." There are a lot of options and various price points from brands you've never heard, and it was hard to tell what features each one had without combing through the listings in detail. The AI assistant helped in a low-information environment like that. The Globluum in an adult's hand (my son does not actually listen to Bob Seger, at least not willingly). Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider That's how I ended up with the Globluum MP3 player for kids. And now, dear friend (we're friends now, aren't we?), I'm recommending it to you. To be clear, there's some downsides: Battery life isn't great. Its listing says 25 hours of playtime, but it definitely runs down faster if you have the screen on. The operating system is slow and laggy. This isn't a $1,000 iPhone! The weird "kid-friendly" design of the apps is kind of uncool and a tween probably wishes it just looked like normal app logos instead of something babyish. Is this the greatest device ever? Absolutely not. No offense to the fine folks at Globluum (hilarious name), but it definitely feels cheap and sort of crappy. But its job is to do one thing (play music) and it does that one thing. At around $70, the price point was about as high as I wanted to go for this kind of device, especially since I suspect there's a high risk of it getting lost or damaged. Anyway, I solved this problem for you! Enjoy!!!! Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Mark Zuckerberg's Thanksgiving menu: 'GTA 6,' smoked meat, and Meta's AI gadget
summary: Mark Zuckerberg shared a Thanksgiving video showing him playing "GTA 6" while Meta's Muse AI agent kept track of his turkey.
content: Mark Zuckerberg didn't miss an opportunity to promote Muse Charm. Bloomberg/Getty Images Mark Zuckerberg shared a Thanksgiving video showing him playing "GTA 6" as a turkey smoked. He asked Meta's Muse AI agent for an update on the bird using a Muse Charm. Zuckerberg said his AI-assisted turkey won his family's annual turkey smoking competition. Mark Zuckerberg found time for a very Mark Zuckerberg "GTA 6" side quest this Thanksgiving: promoting Meta's AI hardware. In a video posted Thursday by Zuckerberg, his wife, Priscilla Chan, enters the room and reminds him that guests will arrive soon. "You're supposed to be making the turkey," Chan says. Zuckerberg is sitting on the sofa playing "GTA 6." Instead of answering her directly, Zuckerberg asks his Muse Charm — a pocket-sized device for speaking with Muse, Meta's AI agent — for an update. Muse says the turkey is on track, its breast temperature is rising steadily, and the smoker is holding near the target. Pulling the turkey around 4 p.m. should leave enough time for the guests, the agent says. Zuckerberg nods and gets back to the game. "Tried a new strategy and got Muse to smoke my turkey this year," Zuckerberg wrote in the Instagram post's caption. He said the result was so good that Chan conceded their annual turkey-smoking competition and asked Muse to smoke hers, too. He also shared a photo of the finished bird on his Instagram story. The holiday promo comes as Muse has proven a hit for Meta. It quickly soared straight to the top of the App Store following its September launch and has been used by more than 10 million people. The technology promises to handle tasks on users' behalf, so they have more time for other pursuits — in Zuck's case, cruising around "GTA 6's" Vice City. Meta unveiled Muse Charm in late September, but it's not yet available for purchase. The standalone gadget gives users voice access to Muse, which Meta says can carry out tasks across connected apps and websites. Zuckerberg is among the millions getting in on the "GTA 6" hype. title: From Waymo to Jeff Bezos' Prometheus, meet the biggest fundraisers in robotics and physical AI
summary: Robotics and physical AI funding hit $97.3 billion so far in 2026, more than double 2025's total.
content: Jeff Bezos Kimberly White/Getty Images for Semafor Robotics and physical AI funding hit $97.3 billion so far in 2026, more than double 2025’s total. Waymo and Jeff Bezos’ Prometheus landed funding rounds of $16 billion and $12 billion, respectively. The boom spans established businesses, defense companies, and early bets on humanoids. From robotaxis and military drones to humanoids that might someday fold your laundry , Silicon Valley is betting billions on a future filled with robots. 2026 was a record year for funding. So far, robotics and physical AI companies have raised $97.3 billion dollars across more than 1,200 deals globally — more than double the $47.4 billion raised in all of 2025, according to Crunchbase. The funding boom spans established businesses like Waymo and early bets on humanoids from companies like Neura Robotics . Defense companies, particularly drone makers such as Anduril, Shield AI, Helsing, and Saronic, account for some of the biggest rounds. Gené Teare, a research lead at Crunchbase, told Business Insider that drones attract more capital because the technology is more mature than other experimental areas of robotics. Sanjay Aggarwal, a partner at VC firm F-Prime, pointed to four drivers of the boom: growth in autonomous vehicles and defense, a push to revive domestic manufacturing, bets on "once-in-a-generation" founders like Jeff Bezos and Travis Kalanick, and futuristic technologies like humanoids. Aggarwal expects the first three categories to keep attracting big checks in 2027, while investors scrutinize the fourth more closely. "You can only raise money on the promise of future revenue for so long," he said. Here are the 10 robotics and physical AI companies that have raised the most funding this year, according to data from Crunchbase. 1. Waymo: $16 billion Waymos in Santa Monica Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Waymo landed the sector's biggest round of the year so far, and its robots are hard to miss. Its Jaguar robotaxis and new Ojai vehicles trundle along practically every block in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Phoenix. It operates in 15 US cities , with more planned for 2027. Its $16 billion Series D, announced in February, valued Waymo at $126 billion. Dragoneer Investment Group, DST Global, and Sequoia Capital led the round, with backing from Alphabet, its majority investor. 2. Prometheus: $12 billion Jeff Bezos is back in the CEO seat. The Amazon founder co-leads Prometheus with former Google X executive Vik Bajaj, marking his first CEO role since leaving Amazon in 2021. The company is building an "artificial general engineer" — AI to help engineers develop and test products from smartphones to jet engines in computer simulations — before manufacturing them in the real world. Its $12 billion Series B, announced in June, valued the company at roughly $41 billion. Investors included Bezos himself, JPMorgan, BlackRock, and Goldman Sachs. 3. Anduril Industries: $5 billion Palmer Luckey Adam Gray/Getty Images for The New York Times Palmer Luckey cofounded his defense tech company nearly a decade ago to build machines for the battlefield. Today, its surveillance towers are deployed along the US-Mexico border, and the company says it has delivered hundreds of Altius drones to Ukrainian forces. The company said it brought in $2.2 billion in revenue last year, more than double its 2024 revenue. Its $5 billion Series H, announced in May, doubled its valuation to $61 billion. Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital led the round. 4. Shield AI: $4 billion Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI builds military drones and Hivemind, an AI pilot for aircraft. Its V-BAT surveillance drone takes off vertically and can fly even in the presence of signal jamming. It helped the US Coast Guard seize $362 million worth of cocaine last year and flew more than 200 missions in Ukraine in 2025. This year, Shield AI raised two $2 billion rounds of financing. In March, the company raised a Series G round led by Advent International and JPMorgan Chase. In November, it announced plans to raise another $2 billion from investors to help fund the acquisition of radar maker Echodyne. The package includes a $1 billion Series H valuing Shield AI at $28.8 billion, plus a separate $1 billion equity investment from Blackstone-managed funds. 5. Zipline International: $2.3 billion Zipline drone Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Zipline began delivering blood in Rwanda in 2016. Today, its drones carry everything from medical supplies to takeout. The company says it has made more than a million deliveries in Dallas-Fort Worth alone this year and is working with Walmart to add 300 delivery sites across the US. Its $1.5 billion Series I, announced this month, valued Zipline at $21.5 billion. Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global led the round. That followed an $800 million Series H that closed in March. 6. Helsing: $1.8 billion Munich-based defense tech company Helsing builds AI software and hardware for military and national security use, including drones and autonomous underwater vehicles. Its HX-2 drone uses AI to navigate and identify targets even when GPS signals are jammed. The company said thousands had been deployed to Ukrainian forces in the first half of 2026 . Its $1.8 billion Series E, announced in July , valued the company at $18 billion. Investors included Dragoneer Investment Group, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and ICONIQ Capital. 7. Saronic: $1.75 billion Austin-based Saronic builds boats designed to operate without crews for the US military and its allies. In June, one of its drone boats, operated by the US Navy, helped rescue two American soldiers after Iran shot down their helicopter off the coast of Oman. The company's $1.75 billion Series D, announced in March , valued it at $9.25 billion. Kleiner Perkins led the round. 8. Atoms: $1.7 billion Travis Kalanick Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick publicly unveiled Atoms earlier this year after years of operating in stealth. The Los Angeles-based company has revealed few details but says it is building robots for food, mining, and transportation. It also absorbed Kalanick's ghost-kitchen business, CloudKitchens , as a subsidiary. Atoms announced a $1.7 billion funding round on July 22, led by Andreessen Horowitz, to pursue what Kalanick called "a journey to digitize the physical world." 9. Skild AI: $1.4 billion Founded by Carnegie Mellon researchers Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta, Pittsburgh-based Skild AI is building an AI model capable of controlling machines ranging from robotic arms to humanoids. Its model is designed to help different robots learn new jobs without being programmed for each task. Skild said in September that it had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue from more than 60 customers. Projects include robotic assembly with Nvidia and Foxconn and kitchen pilots with Mitsui. Its $1.4 billion Series C, announced on January 14, valued Skild at more than $14 billion. SoftBank Group led the round. 10. Neura Robotics: $1.4 billion Neura Robotics Sven Hoppe/picture alliance via Getty Images Germany's Neura Robotics builds robotic arms and mobile carts and is developing humanoids. Customers can rent space at its "robot gyms" — training centers equipped with simulators and tracking technology — to teach machines specific jobs, then transfer those skills to other robots. Its $1.4 billion Series C, announced in June, was led by Tether Investments, with backing from Amazon, Nvidia, and Bosch. Have a tip? title: The military tested robots to help medics find wounded troops and decide who needs help first
summary: Drones and ground robots searched mock disaster zones in a military test to help medics find wounded troops and prioritize lifesaving care.
content: Medics working alongside a ground robot prepare to treat simulated casualties during a DARPA Triage Challenge event in September 2025. The competition concluded earlier this month. Paul Flacks/DARPA Drones and robots had 15 minutes to find mock casualties in a major medical triage challenge. Machines assessed injuries and evacuation priorities without touching patients. The goal is to help combat medics prioritize care when supplies and evacuation are limited. Earlier this month, drones and ground robots searched simulated disaster zones in a competition testing whether machines could help military medics quickly find casualties and identify which needed lifesaving care first. It was all part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency's "Triage Challenge," an event meant to test companies and universities on whether their tech could be a viable solution for medics on future battlefields filled with enemy drones and AI. DARPA is the Pentagon's research arm tasked with finding potential answers to tough military problems, like how missiles can strike their targets when GPS disappears and how to stop adversaries from wrecking havoc on economic markets . At the Disaster City facility in College Station, Texas, a facility built to replicate disasters to test emergency response teams, medics and robots faced scenarios like responding to tornado destruction and a nighttime attack on a military outpost. Ground robots and drones had 15 minutes to find actors and mannequins representing wounded troops and civilians. In another test, they were given the casualties' locations and had five minutes to assess how urgently they needed help. A medic and an unmanned ground vehicle search for casualties as an planned explosion detonates in the background, part of the DARPA Triage Challenge on Nov. 13th, in College Station, Texas. Paul Flacks/DARPA The machines also had to identify injuries, check whether casualties responded, and decide who needed to be evacuated first — all without touching patients. Jeremy Pamplin, the event's program manager and a retired Army physician, told Business Insider in September that rapid triage focused on severe bleeding and breathing problems, identifying someone a medic needed to reach immediately. "Teams have to get out there, recognize these problems really fast and say, 'yep, that's somebody you got to go see right now," he said. Robots and drones could help medics find "needles in the haystack," he said of simulated patients, "to try to save the most lives they possibly can." Military officials have previously warned that the US military is unlikely to control the air in future conflicts, potentially leading to major casualty evacuation challenges the US military has not experienced in decades. That prospect has prompted medical units to begin training to treat frontline casualties for days, or even weeks, before they might receive advanced care. Drones scouted ahead of medics and ground robots, sending casualty information to the medics' phones. A separate element of the event tested whether algorithms could predict what treatment patients would need hours later. In a major war, medics may have to focus scarce resources on casualties they can save, an ethical dilemma most medical providers in the US military have little experience confronting. Pamplin hopes technology can help medics make such decisions with better information. Robots could locate and assess casualties while predictive algorithms help medics anticipate what treatment each patient needs and how long they can wait. That type of mechanical help might aid medics not just by saving more lives, he said, but also by "relieving the burden of doubt from our young medics and war fighters as they're trying to manage those situations."
