title: The most iconic burger joint in every state
summary: From classic diners and sit-down restaurants to drive-thrus, here are the most iconic burger restaurants across the country.
content: From classic diners and sit-down restaurants to drive-thrus, here are the most iconic burger restaurants across the country. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Famous burger joints can be found in every corner of the country. We found the most famous burger restaurants nationwide based on local lore and reviews. From nostalgic drive-ins to local institutions, here's the most iconic burger joint in every state. When the weather turns colder, a hot, juicy burger is one of the best ways to warm up. We found the most iconic or best-known burger joints in every state, from nationally known institutions like In-N-Out Burger in California to tiny roadside stands that have become local legends. Our list includes burger destinations with historical or regional significance and devoted local or national followings. Many have been serving their signature patties for decades, earned major accolades, or been featured on TV — proof that an unforgettable burger can be found in every corner of the country. Here's the most iconic burger joint in every state. ALABAMA: Vicki's Lunch Van in Montgomery Vicki's Lunch Van. Jamie V./Yelp Vicki's Lunch Van isn't much to look at from the outside, but that's part of the charm of this no-frills Montgomery institution. Open since 2003, it's best known for thick, hand-patted burgers that are much bigger than you'd expect from a place called a lunch van, served simply with classic toppings and golden fries. ALASKA: Arctic Roadrunner in Anchorage Arctic Roadrunner. Andrew H./Yelp Arctic Roadrunner has been feeding Anchorage since 1964, when Richard Sanchis started selling cheeseburgers from a trailer before opening a permanent restaurant. Its burgers feature names inspired by the state, such as the Kenai Whopper and Kodiak Islander, while longtime customers can even earn a spot in the restaurant's photo gallery, which spans over 20 years of visits. ARIZONA: The Chuckbox in Tempe The Chuck Box. Travis T./Yelp The Chuckbox has been grilling burgers in Tempe since 1972, and thankfully, not much has changed. Burgers are still cooked over an open mesquite fire, giving them their signature smoky char, and the restaurant remains cash-only. Locals recommend the Tijuana Torpedo, topped with jalapeño jack cheese and green chile, for a burger with distinctly Southwestern heat. ARKANSAS: Hugo's in Fayetteville Hugo's. Paige C./Yelp You have to head underground to find one of Arkansas' most beloved burgers. Located in a basement just off Fayetteville's historic square since 1977, Hugo's has become a longtime hangout for generations of University of Arkansas students. Its burgers, homemade fries, beer-cheese soup, and famously retro atmosphere have helped make the restaurant a Fayetteville institution. CALIFORNIA: In-N-Out Burger in Baldwin Park In-N-Out Burger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider California's most iconic burger is also one of its most widely available — at least in the state; not so much elsewhere in the country. Harry and Esther Snyder opened the first location in Baldwin Park in 1948, where the restaurant's two-way speaker system helped pioneer the drive-thru ordering experience. More than 75 years later, the tiny menu, Double-Double, Animal Style fries, and red-and-yellow branding are practically synonymous with Southern California. COLORADO: My Brother's Bar in Denver My Brother's Bar. John C./Yelp My Brother's Bar has only had its current name since 1970, but people have been drinking at its Denver address since 1873, making it one of the city's oldest continuously operating bars. Today, it's nearly as famous for burgers like the three-cheese Johnny Burger and buffalo-bison Ralphie burger as it is for its lengthy history. CONNECTICUT: Louis' Lunch in New Haven Louis' Lunch. Nolan F./Yelp Louis' Lunch has one of the strongest claims to inventing the hamburger, so naming it Connecticut's most iconic burger joint was a no-brainer. The Lassen family says Louis Lassen first put ground steak between slices of toast for a customer in a rush way back in 1900. The restaurant still cooks its burgers in antique vertical broilers and serves them on toast with only cheese, tomato, or onion available as toppings. DELAWARE: The Charcoal Pit in Wilmington Charcoal Pit. Wilton P./Yelp The Charcoal Pit looks like the kind of burger joint you'd see in a 1950s movie … except it really has been around since 1956. Flame-broiled burgers, triple-spun milkshakes, red booths, and a giant neon sign have made the local restaurant a nostalgic favorite for generations of Delaware diners. The restaurant's customers over the years have included US presidents, including Barack Obama and Delaware native Joe Biden, who has been going for years. FLORIDA: El Cap in St. Petersburg El Cap Restaurant. Michelle T./Yelp There are plenty of flashy places to grab a burger in Florida, but El Cap has become a St. Petersburg favorite by being pretty much the opposite. The old-school neighborhood joint keeps its burgers straightforward, serving thin patties with classic toppings like lettuce and tomato alongside pints of ice-cold beer. GEORGIA: Holeman and Finch in Atlanta Holeman and Finch Public House. King R./Yelp Holeman and Finch turned its burger into an Atlanta legend by making it almost impossible to get at first. After opening in 2008, the restaurant famously served just 24 burgers at 10 p.m. each night, prompting crowds to gather for a chance to try it. The double cheeseburger became so popular that it eventually made its way onto the regular menu. HAWAII: Teddy's Bigger Burgers in Honolulu Teddy's Bigger Burgers. Jen K./Yelp Teddy's Bigger Burgers grew out of backyard cookouts before founders Ted Tsakiris and Rich Stula opened their first restaurant near Diamond Head in 1998. The homegrown chain became known for big, charbroiled burgers topped with everything from avocado to grilled pineapple. After decades of local "best burger" recognition and expansion beyond Hawaii, Teddy's remains one of the islands' biggest burger success stories. IDAHO: Hudson's Hamburgers in Coeur d'Alene Hudson's Hamburgers. Jennifer T./Yelp Hudson's Hamburgers has been keeping things simple since Harley Hudson opened his first burger stand in Coeur d'Alene in 1907. The menu has barely changed in more than a century: Burgers come with pickles and onions, and you still won't find fries or milkshakes. Five generations of the Hudson family have worked the grill, making this tiny counter spot a piece of Idaho history. ILLINOIS: Au Cheval in Chicago Au Cheval. Jenni W./Yelp Au Cheval has only been around since 2012, but its burger didn't need long to become a Chicago icon. Bon Appétit raved about it almost immediately, calling the griddled burger — stacked with American cheese, Dijonnaise, and pickles — potentially its favorite in the country and "just about perfect." The resulting hype helped turn long waits into part of the Au Cheval experience. INDIANA: Powers Hamburgers in Fort Wayne Powers Hamburgers. Andrew C./Yelp Powers Hamburgers has been slinging tiny sliders in Fort Wayne since 1940, when founder Leo Powers sold them for only a nickel apiece. The burgers are still made with thin beef patties, cooked with a generous pile of sliced onions, and served on steamed buns. The original 20-seat diner with a wraparound counter is the last surviving location of what was once a larger regional chain. IOWA: Dixie's Biergarten in Decorah Dixie's Biergarten. R A./Yelp Dixie's Biergarten is a newcomer to Iowa's burger scene, but it already has a pretty convincing claim to fame: Its smashburger was named Iowa's Best Burger in 2026 by the Iowa Beef Industry Council . The winning burger stacks two chuck-and-brisket patties with American cheese, fried onions, pickles, lettuce, tomato, and house smash burger sauce. KANSAS: The Cozy Inn in Salina Cozy Inn. TY Y./Yelp If the smell of onions doesn't hit you before you enter the Cozy Inn, it certainly will once you're inside. The six-seat Salina institution has been making tiny, onion-laden sliders since 1922, when they sold for just 5 cents each. More than a century later, the menu is still remarkably simple, and ordering a sack of sliders remains a Kansas tradition. KENTUCKY: Laha's Red Castle in Hodgenville Laha's Red Castle. Tarheel F./Yelp Opened in 1934, Laha's Red Castle is the kind of old-school burger joint where watching your lunch hit the griddle is half the experience. The tiny Hodgenville diner is known for thin, juicy burgers cooked with onions on a well-seasoned griddle right behind the counter, filling the restaurant with the smell of sizzling beef and caramelized onions. The patties are small enough that regulars often order them as doubles or triples, stacked on soft buns for a simple, old-school burger that hasn't needed much updating over the years. LOUISIANA: Port of Call in New Orleans Port Of Call. Anthony R./Yelp Port of Call started as a small neighborhood steakhouse in 1963, but these days, its burgers are just as famous as its steaks. The French Quarter institution serves massive half-pound burgers alongside loaded baked potatoes and has collected numerous local "best burger" honors over the years. MAINE: Fat Boy Drive-In in Brunswick Fat Boy Drive In. Conrad J./Yelp Fat Boy Drive-In has been serving burgers from its retro Brunswick drive-in since 1955. The restaurant spent more than 50 years under the same family before changing hands in 2020, with its new owner pledging to preserve the nostalgic experience and simple menu of burgers, fries, and homemade-tasting milkshakes. MARYLAND: Abbey Burger Bistro in Baltimore Abbey Burger Bistro. Jennifer C./Yelp You can have it your way at this Baltimore burger bar. Opened in Baltimore's Federal Hill neighborhood in 2008, Abbey Burger Bistro features a choose-your-own-adventure approach to burgers. Customers can select everything from classic beef to more unusual proteins and then work through a checklist of buns, cheeses, sauces, and toppings to create their ideal burger. MASSACHUSETTS: White Hut in West Springfield White Hut. Jason P./Yelp White Hut is a Western Massachusetts institution built around one gloriously simple formula: thin burgers, griddled onions, and soft buns. Since it opened in 1939, generations of locals have crowded around the counter for its inexpensive burgers, often topped with the restaurant's signature fried onions and melted white American cheese. MICHIGAN: Motz's Burgers in Detroit Motz's Burgers. Motz's Burgers/Yelp The name of this iconic burger joint has changed over the decades, but Motz's says the style of its famous sliders hasn't. Originally the location of a White Castle, Motz's traces its history to 1929, when its flagship location opened on Fort Street. Its little burgers are still made with fresh beef and onions, then paired with crispy shoestring fries, onion rings, and classic milkshakes for an appropriately old-school Detroit meal. MINNESOTA: Matt's Bar and Grill in Minneapolis Matt's Bar. Devin B./Yelp You can't talk about Minnesota burgers without talking about the Jucy Lucy , and Matt's Bar has one of the strongest claims to inventing it. The restaurant says the cheese-stuffed burger was born shortly after it opened in 1954, when a customer asked for cheese to be sealed between two patties and exclaimed that it was "one juicy Lucy" after taking a bite. MISSISSIPPI: Stamps Super Burgers in Jackson Stamps Super Burgers. A R./Yelp Stamps began as a Jackson grocery store purchased by Algernon Stamps Sr. in 1970, before the family eventually shifted its focus from groceries to burgers. The family has long been known for its thick, generously sized beef patties. Three generations of the family have continued the tradition. MISSOURI: Town Topic Hamburgers in Kansas City Town Topic. Mike M./Yelp Town Topic has been serving burgers since 1937, when two former White Castle employees opened the original Kansas City location and sold hamburgers for just 5 cents. The thin, griddled burgers proved so popular that the business expanded, though today its historic locations retain the feel of old-school lunch or diner counters. MONTANA: The Burger Dive in Billings The Burger Dive. Nick S./Yelp The Burger Dive is famous for its berry-topped burger, invented by owner Brad Halsten, which won the burger category at the 2016 World Food Championships, the Billings Gazette reported. The "I'm Your Huckleberry" burger combines Angus beef with huckleberry-Hatch chile barbecue sauce, bacon, goat cheese, roasted red pepper mayo, and arugula. NEBRASKA: Dinker's in Omaha Dinkers Bar and Grill. Ken C./Yelp Dinker's started as a South Omaha bar in 1965, when founder Frank "Dinker" Synowiecki added a hot plate to serve hungry factory workers coming off overnight shifts. Burgers eventually became the bar's main attraction, with a long list of toppings and combinations turning the neighborhood bar into one of Omaha's best-known burger destinations. Decades later, it still feels much more like a neighborhood watering hole than a polished burger restaurant, which is part of the local appeal. NEVADA: Best Burger in Las Vegas Best Burger. Chiqui A./Yelp In a city packed with celebrity-chef restaurants and over-the-top casino dining, Best Burger keeps things refreshingly simple. The 24-hour Las Vegas spot is known for straightforward cheeseburgers, patty melts, fries, and thick milkshakes, making it as useful for a go-to lunch as it is for a very late-night Vegas meal. NEW HAMPSHIRE: Papa Joe's Humble Kitchen in Milford Papa Joe's Humble Kitchen. Lisa M./Yelp Chef "Papa Joe," his wife, son, and daughter opened this burger-focused restaurant turned local institution in 2009 after years in the New Hampshire restaurant business. Its burgers are made from the family's signature seasoned, fresh-ground beef, which is then scooped onto the grill and served on toasted buns. Its simplicity has made this tiny burger spot a New Hampshire favorite. NEW JERSEY: White Manna in Hackensack White Manna. Chris C./Yelp Few New Jersey burger joints are as instantly recognizable as White Manna, a tiny white building where customers crowd around the griddle to watch their sliders cook. The Hackensack institution is famous for little patties cooked under a mountain of onions, topped with cheese, and tucked into soft potato rolls. They're served on top of a crowded counter, backed by the sizzle of a grill, making the experience distinctly New Jersey. NEW MEXICO: Buckhorn Tavern in San Antonio Buckhorn Tavern. Ken B./Yelp New Mexico takes its green chile cheeseburgers seriously, and the Buckhorn Tavern has one of the state's most famous versions. The Buckhorn Burger piles green chile and cheese onto beef with mustard, lettuce, tomato, onion, and pickles, and famously beat Bobby Flay in a Food Network competition back in 2009. NEW YORK: J.G. Melon in New York City J.G. Melon. Jason S./Yelp J.G. Melon has been serving one of New York City's most famous burgers from its Upper East Side home since 1972. The cheeseburger keeps things classic with a thick, juicy griddled patty on a toasted bun, best paired with the restaurant's signature cottage fries and a Bloody Mary. More than 50 years later, the green-checkered tablecloths, walls adorned with watermelon artwork, and perpetually busy dining room make grabbing a burger here a quintessential New York experience. NORTH CAROLINA: Melvin's Hamburgers & Hot Dogs in Elizabethtown Melvins. Ayana S./Yelp Melvin's has been an Elizabethtown institution since 1938, when it opened as a pool hall that happened to serve burgers and hot dogs. It's now regarded by Southern Living as one of the most beloved burger joints in the South, and the menu is still refreshingly simple. Order the burger "all the way," and it comes topped Carolina-style with mustard, chili, onions, and the restaurant's closely guarded slaw. NORTH DAKOTA: Sickies Garage Burgers & Brews in Bismarck Sickies Garage Burgers & Brews. Sickies Garage Burgers & Brews/Yelp Sickies Garage doesn't exactly believe in keeping the burger menu short, and that's what's made it one of the most popular spots in a state known for its meat. According to its website, the North Dakota-born concept offers roughly 50 different kinds of burgers, ranging from straightforward cheeseburgers to a Glazed Doughnut Burger that uses exactly the kind of bun you'd guess from its name. OHIO: Swensons Drive-In in Akron Swensons Drive-In. Swensons Drive-In/Yelp Swensons has been an Ohio tradition since 1934, a year after founder Wesley "Pop" Swenson started selling burgers from his station wagon. Its signature Galley Boy burger stacks two patties with two secret sauces and tops the bun with a single green olive, while employees still bring orders directly to customers' cars, car-hop style. OKLAHOMA: Sid's Diner in El Reno Sid's Diner. Jeanie O./Yelp Sid's Diner has famously kept the tradition of the fried onion burger alive with its signature offering, which sees cheap onions pressed into beef to stretch patties further and create what became one of Oklahoma's defining foods. Sid's even helped launch El Reno's very own annual Burger Day in 1989, a tradition that's celebrated each year with a gigantic fried onion burger. OREGON: Five Stars Family Burger in Cornelius Five Stars Family Burger. Jonathan Y./Yelp Five Stars Family Burger puts an Oregon-meets-Korea spin on the neighborhood burger joint. The restaurant has earned accolades, including being ranked by Yelp as Oregon's best burger joint. Alongside classic cheeseburgers made with local beef and Tillamook cheese, the family-run Cornelius restaurant serves burgers incorporating kimchi and bulgogi, reflecting the Yim family's Korean roots. PENNSYLVANIA: Lucky's Last Chance in Philadelphia Lucky's Last Chance. Becca D./Yelp Lucky's Last Chance isn't afraid to get weird with a burger, and that's exactly what made it stand out in a city better known for its melted cheesesteaks. This iconic burger joint's PB & Bacon burger tops thick beef patties with peanut butter, American cheese, and bacon, with grape jelly on the side. The burger is so popular that it has twice won the People's Choice award at the Philadelphia Burger Brawl. RHODE ISLAND: Harry's on the Hill in Providence Harry's on the Hill. Harry's on the Hill/Yelp Harry's proves you don't need a giant patty to make a memorable burger. The Providence spot specializes in freshly ground sliders served two at a time. Throw in a craft beer or boozy milkshake, and you'll see why Harry's has turned the humble slider into one of Rhode Island's signature burger experiences. SOUTH CAROLINA: Little Jack's Tavern in Charleston Little Jack's Tavern. Allison R./Yelp Opened in 2016, Little Jack's Tavern may look more like a classic, old-school neighborhood steakhouse in the historic city of Charleston, but its burger has become the real celebrity. The Tavern Burger keeps things nice and simple with a thin griddled patty, American cheese, onions, sauce, and a sesame bun. Bon Appétit helped to put the burger on the national map, telling readers to "ignore the alluring steaks section of the menu in favor of the thin four-ounce patty," which the magazine said "evokes a drive-thru burger in the best possible way." SOUTH DAKOTA: Sugar Shack in Deadwood Sugar Shack. Jim S./Yelp The Sugar Shack is the kind of roadside burger spot you'll always remember fondly from your cross-country road trip. The tiny, casual restaurant outside Deadwood is known for big, juicy burgers served with little fuss, drawing locals, bikers, and travelers exploring the area and the Black Hills. TENNESSEE: Dyer's Burgers in Memphis Dyer's Burgers. Ray G./Yelp Dyer's Burgers has been a Memphis institution since 1912, and its unusual cooking method is a big reason. The burgers are deep-fried in cooking grease that the restaurant says has been continuously strained and replenished since founder Elmer "Doc" Dyer made the first batch more than a century ago. That means the original grease isn't literally still being used to fry its burgers — fresh grease is added as needed, but still preserving what Dyer's calls its "century-old flavor." TEXAS: Dirty Martin's Place in Austin Dirty Martin's Place. Dirty Martin's Place/Yelp Dirty Martin's has been feeding Austin since 1926, when John Martin opened what was then called Martin's Kum Bak Place. It had eight stools and a literal dirt floor, which eventually inspired its name. Since then, generations of University of Texas students have come for griddled burgers, including the O.T. Special, which the restaurant says was Austin's first bacon cheeseburger. UTAH: Lucky 13 in Salt Lake City Lucky 13. Jose T./Yelp Lucky 13 certainly isn't the only burger restaurant in Salt Lake, but it's got one of the most creative menus. From the Nut Butter Burger, topped with peanut butter, bacon, and cheddar, to the habanero-loaded Ring of Fire, the burgers on this menu are anything but simple, earning them a statewide reputation. VERMONT: Worthy Burger in South Royalton Worthy Burger. Emma B./Yelp Worthy Burger has been serving burgers in South Royalton since 2012. The farm-to-table restaurant cooks grass-fed Vermont beef over a hardwood fire for a signature smoky flavor, then tops its Worthy Burger with locally made Plymouth cheddar and house-made special sauce. Its commitment to local ingredients is just one reason the spot has become a favorite among Vermont burger lovers. VIRGINIA: Burger Bar in Bristol Burger Bar. Ida M./Yelp Burger Bar has been serving burgers in downtown Bristol since 1942, making it one of the most historic burger restaurants in the state. The restaurant is also tied to country-music history. Legend has it that Hank Williams ate his final meal there before he died in 1953, though the details of the story have been debated. Today, the restaurant leans into that connection with burgers named after Williams' songs while continuing to serve classic burgers, fries, and shakes in a diner-like setting. WASHINGTON: Frisko Freeze in Tacoma Frisko Freeze. Amanda B./Yelp Frisko Freeze has been serving burgers, fries, and milkshakes from its tiny Tacoma drive-in since 1950. The building and its distinctive neon sign are so closely tied to the city that Frisko Freeze was even added to the Tacoma Register of Historic Places in 2008, a local news source reported at the time. More than 75 years after opening, customers still line up for its classic cheeseburgers and old-school drive-in experience. WEST VIRGINIA: Hillbilly Hot Dogs in Lesage Hillbilly Hot Dogs. Dan W./Yelp While you definitely want to also try a signature hot dog at this quirky roadside restaurant, its burgers come with similarly over-the-top toppings. The restaurant has also become a West Virginia tourist attraction thanks to its collection of old school buses, license plates, signs, and other Appalachian-themed decor, drawing visitors from near and far. WISCONSIN: Solly's Grille in Glendale Solly's Grille. Viv P./Yelp Solly's Grille has been serving Wisconsin's signature butter burgers since 1936. The iconic local burger features fresh sirloin topped with stewed onions and a generous amount of Wisconsin butter that melts across the patty and bun, earning a reputation for its juiciness. In fact, the burger is so famous that the James Beard Foundation named Solly's an America's Classics winner in 2022, recognizing the family-owned diner's place in Wisconsin food history. WYOMING: The Bird in Jackson The Bird. Clay E./Yelp The Bird opened in Jackson in 2010 and has become a popular local stop for burgers, beer, and views of the surrounding mountains. Its half-pound burgers are made with freshly ground beef and served on English muffins rather than traditional burger buns. The restaurant has been awarded gold for Best Burger in Jackson Hole for eight consecutive years. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: He chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. Now he runs his own restaurant in China.
summary: Zhu Guanlin's parents were shocked when he chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. They didn't see being a chef as a stable career path.
content: Zhu Guanlin studied at a culinary school in the US, but when it was time to open his own restaurant, he chose China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Zhu Guanlin, now 32, came from a family of engineers, but chose to attend culinary school in the US. He worked at Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and San Francisco before moving back to China. In 2025, he opened his own restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zhu Guanlin, 32, head chef and owner of Plum, a restaurant in Dali, China. It has been edited for length and clarity. During my final year studying engineering in China , I was in a constant state of anxiety as I prepared to pursue a master's degree. Near where I lived was a small morning market by the river. In China, the northeast is cold, so all the seafood and freshwater fish were laid out in the open, frozen solid. There were freshly slaughtered pigs, and steam still rising from the meat. As people gathered for breakfast, I'd smell deep-fried foods mixing with the scent of bean-flour flatbreads. The air felt alive with the warmth of daily life. It wasn't just the act of cooking that I loved, but the stories behind the food. Why do people in Sichuan eat spicy food , for instance? It's because of the humidity. I realized that by becoming a chef, I could learn it all. Breaking away I was 21 when I received two acceptance letters: one to study electrical engineering at a university in Virginia, and the other from the Culinary Institute of America. Going back to my grandfather's generation, everyone in my family had been an electrical engineer. I was the first to break away from that path. My decision to go to culinary school was a shock to my parents. I hadn't told them that I'd applied. The idea of being a chef felt foreign to them, and they didn't consider it a stable career. Do you have any regrets about a move abroad ? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I moved to New York City in 2019 for a two-year associate degree program. My tuition was nearly $40,000 a year. My parents paid for the first year, but I didn't want to continue taking money from them. I started working, and with the help of a scholarship, I paid for the rest of my time abroad myself. He got internships at Michelin-starred restaurants through Curricular Practical Training, a work authorization available to some international students on F-1 visas. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My school is often called the West Point of the culinary world I met a lot of classmates who were retired Special Forces soldiers or Army infantrymen. We joked that we could only use three phrases: "Yes, Chef," "No, Chef," and "I will do better, Chef." The school allowed internships through Curricular Practical Training (CPT), so I was able to work legally in the US . After finishing two semesters, I spent the third working in restaurants, taking on multiple jobs. After graduating, I did stints at various Michelin-starred restaurants, first in New York and later in San Francisco. During my time in the US, the highest position I reached was chef de partie, the supervisor of a specific station. He moved to Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, to help a former classmate. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My OPT visa was set to expire in about six months I also realized that unless I became a sous chef or chef de cuisine, I wouldn't grow professionally. After seeing the realities up close, Michelin restaurants also lost their aura of mystique. The things I truly cared about, like the culture behind cuisine, were rooted in China . At the end of 2023, a classmate of mine opened a restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, and I went to help co-manage it. Business was quiet at first, but after about six months, it took off. But I wanted to open a restaurant of my own, so I left. In February 2025, I opened Plum in Dali, investing 400,000 Chinese yuan, or about $60,000. The restaurant is set in a courtyard, and we have 35 seats in total. The team has grown from four to 10 employees. We don't define ourselves as either Chinese or Western. A single dish might combine Western components, Chinese techniques , and Japanese or Italian influences. I've made a focaccia that incorporates a French-style sauce, then topped it with sautéed porcini mushrooms, Chinese-style. Lately we've been fully booked every day. Based on my current calculations, it'll take about four or five years to break even. In February 2025, Zhu opened Plum, his own restaurant in Dali, China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Making peace with my parents My parents have realized that being an engineer isn't the only career path. I realize now that back then they were afraid I'd have a hard life. Once I understood that, communicating with them became more relaxed. They even helped fund my new restaurant. New York City was the most diverse city I've ever lived in, where you can find the culture of virtually every ethnic group. That's something I miss. I don't miss some of the Michelin restaurants, though. Sometimes, it felt like they were trying to force a narrative onto their menus. In China, I find kitchen culture can sometimes be cliquey. The master-apprentice system is still dominant, and people can sometimes form groups based on clan ties or local culture, rather than welcome newcomers. I'm still exploring what kitchen culture should look like. Restaurant staff in China typically get four days off a month. I give everyone two consecutive days off each week, plus compensatory time off for holidays. When chefs are overworked, they lose focus. The atmosphere was quiet and orderly at school in New York and in many of the Michelin-starred kitchens I worked at. When I first returned to China , I demanded the same from my own staff. But then, at one point, I realized that it wasn't necessary. When people feel a sense of cohesion and genuine appreciation for their work, they naturally take initiative. title: We couldn't agree on a vacation for 13 people. Then the 8-year-old twins suggested something unexpected.
summary: We celebrated my parents' 80th birthdays with a multigenerational family vacation at an Idaho dude ranch. There was something for everyone.
content: Horseback riding with the family on a dude ranch in Idaho. Courtesy of Bill Hallier We wanted to celebrate my parents' 80th birthdays with a vacation for all 13 family members. After struggling to agree on a destination, the youngest kids suggested an Idaho dude ranch. With activities for every age and meals included, everyone could relax and enjoy time together. Around a campfire in an Idaho horse pasture, our family of 13 hummed along with the jovial guitar-strumming folk singer. The kids licked marshmallow-covered fingers under a starry sky, seemingly mesmerized by the fire's shadows dancing on our faces. It's a memory that has stuck in my mind and made me laugh more than once over the past year. Grandma and Grandpa were celebrating their 80th birthday and wanted the entire family along for the ride. That night under the twinkling stars, for a little while, nobody needed to plan anything or wonder what tomorrow would bring. We could just sit together and sing. But getting us there was considerably less harmonious. We had ages ranging from 8 to 80 We all wanted to celebrate together, but agreeing on where to go nearly derailed the whole thing. Everyone had a say. Unfortunately, most of those opinions conflicted . From cruises to beaches and everything in between, we just couldn't decide where to go or what type of vacation would work best for our large group. The author went on a multigenerational trip with her family Courtesy of Bill Hallier With ages ranging from 8 to 80, we were asking a lot of one vacation. The kids needed adventures and time with the other young campers. The teenagers needed some freedom. The adults were hoping to relax, and we all wanted Grandma and Grandpa to enjoy their birthday without spending the trip keeping everyone else entertained. Then the youngest of the group, 8-year-old twins, suggested a dude ranch . It was the idea with the fewest complaints, and in our family, that counted as enthusiasm. What followed was an Idaho getaway reminiscent of the kind of family time I remember from childhood, when we were happy just sitting outside together under the stars. There was plenty to do, but it also allowed us to do very little. Getting there and staying together were manageable Before falling in love with a ranch, we looked at how everyone would get there. A beautiful setting loses some appeal if getting there requires an exhausting journey, especially with young children or older relatives. The author's family was celebrating Grandma and Grandad's 80th. Courtesy of Bill Hallier Our Idaho choice was somewhere everyone could easily fly to . A ranch within driving distance might make more sense, depending on budget and other factors. Starting close to home can help narrow the search. The housing was equally important. Multiple lodging options let us divide up without scattering across the property. The teenagers and young adults could bunk together. Couples had privacy. We could easily see where everyone else was staying, so visiting each other's cabins was as easy as walking a few short steps. Nobody had to enjoy the same things Our ranch offered enough activities that choosing one didn't mean persuading 12 other people to join. There was horseback riding, of course. But there was also a pool for sunbathing. Anyone wanting a challenge could try rock climbing or the ropes activities. Archery and shooting appealed to some, while mountain biking offered a more adventurous way to spend the afternoon. There was something for every family member to do. Courtesy of Bill Hallier Arts and crafts kept the younger kids occupied, and the camp staff kept them busy throughout the day so the adults could have some downtime. That variety took pressure off the trip. We didn't need to turn every morning into a family meeting about the day's agenda. People could head toward what interested them and catch up later. Off-site excursions widened the choices further, including fly-fishing outings a few towns over. Meals gave us an easy place to come back together Feeding 13 people can be the most tedious chore of a vacation. Someone has to find a restaurant, check the menu, and figure out whether it can accommodate everyone. At the ranch, meals were already taken care of. There were plenty of choices, and the staff could accommodate allergies and preferences. We could come together to eat without someone spending the afternoon arranging it. Courtesy of Bill Hallier We could join the fun or take a break Evenings offered another chance to spend time together. There was karaoke in the barn, spa sessions under the stars, and Jeep rides to feed the horses. The staff made those experiences feel personal by learning our names and connecting with us through all the different activities offered. They sang around the campfire and joined the evening dancing to a local band. Their enthusiasm helped us loosen up, too. It had an Americana feel that suited the birthday celebration. Still, togetherness has its limits, even when you love the people involved. Anyone who wanted space could take a walk or fish alone. The pool worked equally well for swimming and lounging, and reading a book with a view was a perfectly respectable way to spend an afternoon. Nobody had to keep pace with the most energetic person in the family. Looking back, the ranch worked because we could spend time together without having to negotiate every hour. We had places to gather and room to wander off. We proved that a multigenerational vacation could work for everyone; it just took a little planning. For Grandma and Grandpa's 80th birthday, we'd wanted everyone there. The dude ranch made it possible for everyone to enjoy being there, too. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: NAPA's solution to America's blue-collar worker shortage: Make training feel like Madden Football
summary: A former "Madden" producer helped developed tech that NAPA thinks could help America's auto tech shortage.
content: NAPA thinks it's found a tech solution that will accelerate the auto tech talent pipeline. NAPA A former "Madden" producer helped NAPA produce its XR goggles and smart glasses. The technology, NAPA hopes, will help build a pipeline of auto tech talent. The training goggles won a SEMA award as shops contend with a technician shortage. NAPA's auto-repair training is taking a page out of "Madden's" book. The auto-parts company has spent the past two-and-a-half years developing a new training platform, called XcceleratoR, with Robin Cowie, the founder and CEO of Skillmaker. XcceleratoR has two core tech products: XR training goggles that place car-fixers inside a virtual shop with a digital pickup and EV, and smart glasses designed to provide repair guidance as they work on real cars. On paper, Cowie looks like a strange talent to call on amid the auto industry's labor problems . He produced the 1999 hit "The Blair Witch Project" and worked for three years as the senior narrative producer for the "Madden NFL" franchise. He says he helped develop tech with some surprising overlap. "Madden is really a football simulator. A lot of professional players play it, a lot of coaches play it, they teach strategy," he said. "What we've created here is a simulation for technicians." The gamified training blitz comes as repair shops face increasingly difficult tasks: finding and training car mechanics with the skills to work on modern vehicles — and then retaining them. NAPA estimates that the US is short roughly 642,000 technicians. A recent study commissioned by Ford says that each year, 66,000 new technician and mechanic jobs open. "With the amount of jobs and people that want technicians in their shop, and the shortage we have, the first thing we've got to worry about is keeping them," Shawn Gilfillan, the owner of New Jersey-based Automotive Magic repair shops, told Business Insider. Gilfillan's shops use NAPA tools. Inside the tech A technician-in-training uses NAPA's XR glasses. NAPA When technicians first put on the goggles, they start next to a virtual tool bin. Connected handle attachments provide haptic feedback as users tighten nuts and bolts. "The physics have to be real, the tools have to be real, the information has to be real," Cowie said about the VR experience. "If you get the wrong piece of information, you don't fix the car." NAPA says the goggles include 53 lessons, 148 hours of training, and preparation for three Automotive Service Excellence certifications. It says trainees can go from "onboarding to billable" in 25 days. The company also says shops can use a 45- to 60-minute goggle-based assessment to gauge a prospective hire's existing competency. The XR Training Goggles won SEMA's 2026 New Product Award for Emerging Technology Product earlier this month. NAPA said the software had exited beta right before the Vegas auto industry conference. The other half of XcceleratoR is designed for the workday. NAPA's smart glasses use voice commands and vehicle-specific repair information to guide technicians through a job without requiring them to repeatedly leave their workstation for a computer terminal. The system draws on NAPA's own knowledge base and repair information from partners including Identifix and AutoVitals. The premise is that their familiar, game-like software could help a fresh batch of technicians build their skills faster — and without forcing them to read the nearly 1,900-page books that trained the old generation of car-fixers. Once the new talent is trained, the glasses can help keep the repair shop flowing. " Cars are extremely complicated . They're rolling computers," Jason Rainey, NAPA's vice president of commercial sales, said. "Now you're taking the actual systems that they were gaming with and using that to apply in a skill set that will last in the next 40 years." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Norse Atlantic once offered $99 flights to Europe. Now it's fighting to avoid being the 2nd big airline casualty of 2026.
summary: Norse Atlantic has previously offered transatlantic flights for $99 but has struggled with surging fuel prices due to the war in Iran.
content: A Norse Atlantic Airways Boeing 787. PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit filed for bankruptcy as it fights to stay in business. It also grounded its flights and received notices terminating the lease agreements for its fleet. Norse had been losing millions since fuel prices surged due to the Iran war. Cheap transatlantic flights are on the brink as Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy. The budget airline, which has previously offered one-way New York-to-London tickets for as little as $99, warned on Wednesday that its "financial situation is critical." On Friday, it announced that its Norwegian operating unit had filed for bankruptcy. All Norse flights are canceled, and ticket sales have been discontinued, it added. "We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners," said CEO Eivind Roald. He added that the board, management, and its advisors are "working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations." Earlier on Friday, Norse said that it received notices terminating the lease agreements for all 12 of its airplanes. It added that while it was contesting these and is still continuing discussions over short-term financing, "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found." Shares in the airline, which trade on the Norwegian stock exchange, are trading at 1 cent, down 40% over the past five days, and 98.5% since the start of the year. The airline reported a net loss of $94.6 million for the first half of the year. It also noted that fuel prices had nearly doubled compared to last year. Before this week, Norse had already been looking for ways to shore up its finances. In May, it announced a cost-cutting plan aimed at saving $50 million a year, including the elimination of 75 jobs. And last August, it axed half of its US-to-Europe routes . Norse was founded in 2021 after fellow Scandinavian carrier Norwegian Air abandoned its transatlantic routes as it fought to survive the pandemic. Norse uses the familiar budget-airline model, relying on extra fees for baggage, seat selection, and onboard meals. However, the war in Iran has sent jet fuel prices skyrocketing. Unlike many European carriers, Norse does not hedge its fuel purchases, so it has been more exposed to the surge. The fuel surge has already brought down another budget carrier. Spirit Airlines shut down in May after filing for bankruptcy protection twice. Spirit CEO Dave Davis said higher fuel prices had left the airline needing hundreds of millions of dollars in extra funding to keep operating. Norse also made money by providing planes and pilots to other airlines. It leased six of its Boeing 787s to IndiGo, an Indian budget airline. But the war disrupted that arrangement, too. Airspace restrictions forced longer flights between India and Europe, while higher fuel costs made the routes more expensive to operate. The two airlines agreed to end the deal, with the planes returning to Norse at the start of November. For now, the fate of Norse's funding talks and its fleet remains uncertain, while passengers are left working out how to complete their journeys without it. title: Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, 59, says his athletic experience helped him through stroke rehab
summary: Four-time Olympic gold medalist Michael Johnson, 59, shared what kept him going through difficult weeks of stroke rehab.
content: Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson says focusing on small gains helped him through stroke rehab. David Madison/Getty Images Former sprinter Michael Johnson says his athletic mindset helped him recover from a stroke. Years of Olympic training helped him spot progress in his recovery that he might otherwise have missed. He said that gave him a reason to keep going when he felt he wasn't getting better. Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, 59, says his mindset as an athlete helped him through stroke rehab . On Wednesday's episode of the " How to Fail with Elizabeth Day " podcast, the four-time Olympic gold medalist spoke about suffering a stroke in 2018, which left him unable to walk and with limited movement in his left arm and fingers. "The rehabilitation was hard, but it was much easier for me because of having been an Olympic athlete," Johnson said. "So many stroke survivors don't make a full recovery or don't make as much of a recovery as they can, because they stop short and they give up," Johnson said. "Because they don't recognize what I was very fortunate to have experience in recognizing — which is how you actually train for these tiny marginal gains every day." Johnson said years of training for small improvements helped him notice daily progress in his recovery that others might have missed. His past athletic training also helped him through weeks when he felt his recovery had stalled. He remembered the same frustration from preparing for the Olympics , when hard work didn't always produce noticeable results. "I know, though, that I got better, and that is the motivation that keeps you going," he added. Johnson said the stroke recovery process was physically demanding and could be disheartening. "When you see that I am a shell of what I used to be in terms of how much weight I can lift, and how much coordination I can have, it's not very uplifting, right?" he said. "But you have to be able to, and that is the same thing again. I had the benefit of having been through it as an athlete." Others have also spoken about the value of small improvements during recovery. Lime CEO Wayne Ting told Business Insider in October that recovering from a stroke, like improving his company's finances, involved getting "1% better" every day. Lessons from sports can carry into other parts of life, too, including work. Goldman Sachs executive and former college lacrosse player Madison Crutchfield told Business Insider in October 2025 that competing taught her to stay levelheaded under pressure and respond constructively when things went wrong. title: I moved from California to Texas and helped others do the same. After the blue wave, I'm heading to Florida.
summary: Realtor Marie Bailey specialized in California to Texas movers. Now she's moving to Florida, and thinks more people will do the same.
content: Marie Bailey moved from California to Texas. Now she's moving to Florida. Marie Bailey Marie Bailey moved from California to Texas and helped over 300 families do the same. Now, the real estate agent is moving to Florida and expanding her business there. After Texas went blue, Bailey said she expects more and more people to choose Florida. This is an as-told-to essay based on a conversation with Marie Bailey, a real estate agent who has helped over 300 families move from California to Texas . The story has been edited for length and clarity. I grew up in Orange County and was living in Los Angeles in 2017 when my family decided to move to Prosper, Texas. The number one reason was the cost of living, and number two was politics. After the 2016 election, it was just so polarizing. Especially in LA, you couldn't say you voted for Trump. We sold a 1,500-square-foot house in Seal Beach for the same price as the big 5,000-square-foot house we built in Texas, across the street from a five-acre manmade crystal lagoon. Texas was also much more conservative. There are people who are not conservative, but it's not as polarizing. People are much more chill than they were in LA, which was nice because at the end of the day, your neighbor is your neighbor. I was not a real estate agent when we moved, but I saw a trend coming in 2018. I decided to be a real estate agent who specializes in helping Californians move to Texas . I was able to share my personal experience. People would come out on scouting trips, and I would have everything mapped out for them and help them decide on areas. I helped over 300 families make the move. After Texas went blue in the midterms, I'm expecting another trend: I think a lot of people are going to move to Florida. I am personally moving to Florida and expanding my team there. I was already considering a move, but the midterms solidified my decision. And I'm hearing from a lot of clients and other relocators that they are also thinking about making the move. The midterms were a shock I started a Facebook page called "Move to Texas from California" that grew to over 45,000 members. I've already changed the page title to "Moving out of California" because more and more people are interested in moving to other places now, like Florida. The election was a shock to all of us. I was completely, utterly shocked. The next day, everyone in my group was posting, "Well, we might have to rethink where we're going." I didn't think Texas was going to go blue, but I did feel a shift happening. Texas making abortion illegal was highly unpopular, even with Republicans, as was making pot a felony. People were disenchanted. I think that's why they lost the election. I don't think it was the Californians that moved here. I think it was those extreme laws that they put in place. I already have one client who has decided not to build a business in Texas after the election. Another client called me and said, "I need to sell my rental house immediately. I don't see this being good for Texas." And that was a native Texan. They're concerned taxes are going to go up, as well as about proposals related to immigration and gun laws. Some people feel like, "Great, we already saw this happen in our state, so we're going to have to rethink things." I don't think there's going to be a huge Exodus yet, but if these policies go through, then a lot of people might move. I'm moving my business to Florida The decision to move for me is not all politics. I have family in Florida and, because I think others will be making the move, it's a business decision as well. I am actively working on getting my Florida real estate license and plan to run a team there. I'm planning to move by the end of the year. I'm still going to manage a team in Texas. It's a lot of work, and moving is stressful, but I'm doing it: moving at the same time as I get my license and build my team. I'm planning to move near The Villages because there are so many people retiring there. I'll continue to specialize on relocators — people moving to Florida from anywhere. Beyond politics, I think a lot of people just want to move to Florida because it's amazing. Orlando is the number one travel destination in the world. One thing I really missed in California was Disneyland, so now I can be closer to Disney World. Texas is still a wonderful place, and I want the best for it no matter what. I hope that turning blue doesn't dissuade businesses from coming to Texas because that really does a lot for the economy. I'm not sad to leave. I'm excited to expand. But I am sad that Texas turned blue. I just see the writing on the wall for what happened in places like California and New York. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I spent a day only using robot services. Here's how I'd rank them.
summary: Business Insider's Lloyd Lee used every robot service he could find in San Francisco, from robotaxis to humanoid cleaning services.
content: Business Insider's Lloyd Lee used robot services throughout San Francisco, including barista bots, robotaxis, and humanoids. Jess Lynn Goss for BI I tried using only robot services for 12 hours in San Francisco, from robotaxis to humanoids. Some robots provided real utility or were at least fun to use. Others made my life more complicated. Here's how I'd rank them. The robots are slowly taking over San Francisco. They're on our roads, our gyms, our coffee shops. Not all of them are useful, however. At least not yet. I spent 12 hours seeking out every robot service I could find that's publicly available. Some provided real utility and shocked me at how competitive their costs were compared to their human-driven counterparts. Others clearly needed to work out their kinks. My ranking is qualitative and listed in order from worst to best. I considered how useful the robots were, how easy they were to use, how much automation is involved, and how much they cost for the consumer. Here's how I rank the robots. Tau Robotics' humanoids Jess Lynn Goss for BI Humanoids remain one of the more challenging technical problems for the robotics industry , and my experience with Tau Robotics' humanoid cleaning service underscored that. For $30 an hour, a human employee from Tau Robotics will bring over two humanoids, which vacuum and mop the floors, clean the toilets, wipe down surfaces, and dust. Cheap, for sure, but not very effective. They left the house in worse condition than it started, knocking over the trash can and a large mirror. In a few cases, the robots simply shut down. They're also mostly teleoperated, meaning they're controlled by a remote human employee — all part of the training process , as the robots continue to gather data. For now, the humanoids need a lot of work. Ohlso's robot kitchen Jess Lynn Goss for BI Ohlso is a Korean food truck trying to solve the problem of cold-delivered food with a "cook-en-route" concept, in which a robot preps the meal as the truck heads to the delivery destination. Humans are still involved in the food prep process, such as marinating the meat or vegetables, before the ingredients are loaded onto the truck. From there, the robots cook up the food. A human also drives the truck and packs up the meals. It's a neat enough idea, but I don't know how well it works in action because the truck was parked the day I tried it. It's hard to see whether the customer sees any cost savings from having robots instead of a human chef. I got a small serving of braised beef short ribs and a lot of rice for about $17. The meat was cooked through and tasted fine. Aescape's robot masseuse Jess Lynn Goss for BI A company called Aescape wants to make massage sessions more accessible and less awkward, and I think it succeeds. You book an appointment online, and then you get a massage by a pair of mechanical arms in the comfort of a private room. A 30-minute session costs $60. That's a decent cost proposition, considering a private massage by a human can run you well over $100. And for the introverts, that could also be attractive. The thing is, the robots need to feel good. I thought the arms applied a good amount of pressure to the body and the heated hands were a nice touch. I just wished I could control exactly where on my body the arms hit. UBTech's robot waiter Jess Lynn Goss for BI Sometimes simple is better. Hikari Sushi & Bar deploys one robot — UBTech's guest service bot , Cadebot — to help the kitchen deliver larger menu items to tables. That's it. That's its sole purpose. The robot wheels over to the table, as it plays a little jingle, delivers the food, and leaves. At least the way Hikari configured it, the robot does not interact with the customer. And honestly, that's fine with me. Artly's barista bots Jess Lynn Goss for BI The coffee at Artly cafe at Pier 30 wasn't notable, but the barista bots do draw latte art in the shape of a rose or a heart better than most of us ever will. My cappuccino was $6.79 — a little disappointing, since a similar-quality drink at Starbucks would run me under $5. Part of the premise of robot labor should be that services are cheaper, right? At least with Artly, there was less pressure to tip. Matic Robot's vacuum Jess Lynn Goss for BI Matic's robot vacuum is a friendly little home helper. It stands about eight inches tall and is much quieter than a typical manual vacuum. The company appears to have thought about the user experience with Apple-like precision from the moment you unbox the machine, making it easy to learn how to use. After the robot does a 3D scan of your home, it's mostly hands-off from there, aside from replacing the vacuum bag or refilling the water tank. It also functions as a mop. The app allows you to schedule cleanups and choose which rooms to vacuum. It doesn't replace manual cleaning. The Matic isn't always strong enough to pick up every stain, and the robot's shape can pose a barrier in some trickier crevices and corners of the home. It's also a pricey piece of homeware: $1,500. A top-line vacuum that's much stronger could run you $500. Waymo's robotaxis Jess Lynn Goss for BI I solely relied on Waymo's driverless ride-hailing service to get to my destinations. And the fact that I was able to rely on it gives Waymo the top spot. Hailing a Waymo is as simple as hailing any ride-hailing service: You open an app and set a destination. And, to my surprise, most rides were cheaper than Uber. I hailed seven rides and spent $124.69 in total, for an average price of $17.81 per ride. The autonomous driver isn't perfect. There were moments during my ride when the robotaxi felt stiff or jerked, as if it were tapping the brakes. Overall, I did get to all my destinations safely. title: 42 state attorneys want to stop Character.ai from auctioning private chat histories to the highest bidder
summary: State attorneys general said that the now-bankrupt AI chatbot company is planning to sell chat histories from 21 million US accounts.
content: Character.AI is planning to sell millions of chat histories, says a group of state attorneys. Illustration by Algi Febri Sugita/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images State attorneys general move to block Character.AI from auctioning millions of private user chats. The objection says that datasets includes account details and sensitive chat histories. They said bankruptcy should not allow Character to sidestep federal and state privacy protections. A group of state attorneys general is asking a bankruptcy court to stop Character.AI from auctioning off millions of users’ private chatbot conversations, including records tied to children, to the highest bidder. In a filing on Tuesday, 42 state attorneys general said that the now- bankrupt AI chatbot company is planning to sell chat histories from 21 million US accounts, more than 2 million of which include children . the December 1 auction would also sell private information such as account details, IP addresses, and other metadata, as well as internal risk scores the company assigned users. The states argue that the terms of sale give users virtually no protection. A buyer would not be required to follow Character.AI’s privacy policy, honor deletion requests, or limit how it uses or resells the data, they said. The attorneys added that Character.AI had previously told users that it did not sell personal information for money. “Character.AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chat histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” Bonta said in a statement. According to the states, the datasets include conversations involving self-harm, eating disorders, suicidal thoughts, sexual material and users who treated characters presenting themselves as therapists or doctors. The coalition asked the court to reject the terms of the sale, and the company’s proposed lead bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, an entity formed in Delaware a day before Character.AI selected it for the role. The states say bankruptcy should not allow Character.AI to sidestep federal and state privacy protections, particularly for children. At minimum, they said, any sale should exclude minors’ chats and other sensitive data and impose meaningful conditions on whoever acquires the company’s assets. Character.AI did not respond to a request for comment. Character.AI’s safety practices have faced intense scrutiny and multiple lawsuits. The company, its founders, and Google were sued by the mother of a Florida teenager who alleged that a chatbot fostered an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship with her 14-year-old son, reinforced his suicidal thoughts, and contributed to his death. Character.AI and Google later reached settlements in teen-harm lawsuits. The startup was founded by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. In 2024, Google struck a roughly $2.7 billion deal for a nonexclusive license to Character.AI’s technology and brought the founders back to the company, while Character.AI continued operating independently. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Young Americans are counting on stocks to build wealth. One economist says there's a catch that could kill this plan.
summary: Younger Americans' growing reliance on stocks to build wealth could limit the Fed's ability to tolerate a market downturn.
content: Younger Americans are increasingly dependent on stock-market performance to build wealth and fund their retirement. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Young Americans increasingly depend on stocks to build wealth as homeownership becomes harder to attain. An economist warns that historical equity returns point to a decade of zero returns. Millennials rely more on investment-based retirement plans than boomers, exposing them to market swings. Young Americans are increasingly dependent on the stock market to build wealth as traditional paths to financial security become harder to access. But one economist warns that historical market returns point to a potentially disappointing decade ahead. Steven Blitz, the chief US economist at GlobalData.TS Lombard, wrote on Wednesday that long-term equity-return data suggest investors should expect zero returns over the next 10 years. The warning comes as younger Americans face barriers to homeownership and savings deposits offer limited returns, leaving them increasingly reliant on equities to accumulate wealth for retirement, Blitz argued. "Households' feeling that the economy fails to deliver is rooted in reality not imagination," Blitz wrote. Millennials are particularly exposed because they rely more heavily on 401(k)-style retirement plans, whose value depends on investment performance, than traditional pensions. Blitz found that millennials have $1.30 in such retirement benefits for every dollar in traditional pension benefits, compared with $1.05 for Gen X and just 59 cents for baby boomers. Millennials also trail baby boomers in their asset-to-liability ratios at comparable life stages, though they are roughly on par with Generation X, according to the report. Blitz argues that the growing importance of equities to household finances has implications for monetary policy. The Federal Reserve traditionally influences economic activity through borrowing and lending costs, but household finances have become increasingly tied to equities rather than credit-driven spending, he said. That dependence could also constrain the Fed's ability to tolerate a sustained stock-market downturn, Blitz wrote, because falling share prices could undermine household wealth and confidence. "The economy is not broken, but it operates very differently, and policy has yet to adapt," Blitz wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving with flight delays, over 960,000 power outages, and a Delta ground stop at LaGuardia
summary: Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled.
content: A storm is hitting the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel with flight delays and cancellations across the US. Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Bad weather has led to the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel and leading to power outages in homes across the East Coast. As of 8:30 p.m. ET Thursday, over 2,300 flights within, into, or out of the US had been delayed and 451 canceled, according to FlightAware. The day before, more than 6,500 flights were delayed and about 160 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. Over 960,000 US households were without power on Thursday evening, according to PowerOutage.us. That included about 124,000 in Virginia, 151,000 in Maryland, about 191,000 in New Jersey, and over 224,000 in Pennsylvania. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. One in four flights departing Baltimore/Washington International were canceled, according to FlightAware. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. On Thursday morning, LaGuardia Airport recorded wind gusts of up to 39 knots, or 45 miles per hour. Such strong winds can disrupt flying. LaGuardia issued a ground stop for aircraft from Delta Air Lines in the evening, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Mamdani said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Disruption was worsened in Miami when a FedEx plane overshot the runway on Wednesday evening. No injuries were reported, though the incident caused inbound flights to be grounded for about 90 minutes. title: Who trusts influencers? These 4 stats reveal the state of creator marketing.
summary: Advertisers are spending billions on influencers. Here are key stats marketers need to know about Americans' attitudes toward creators.
content: Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for Sony Pictures Entertainment How do Americans really feel about influencers? Morning Consult surveyed about 2,000 US adults exclusively for Business Insider. Here are four stats influencer marketers should know — including who trusts influencers the most. Influencer marketing is ultimately powered by one thing: people's feelings. Whether you hit "buy" on an item an influencer is promoting could come down to how much you trust that creator. We wanted to get a gut-check on how Americans feel about influencers. Morning Consult conducted research exclusively for Business Insider and surveyed about 2,000 US adults in September about overall trust, purchase decisions and regrets, politics, and sponsorship disclosures. The biggest takeaway: Feelings about influencers — especially trust — vary greatly by income and generation. For instance, baby boomers often find influencers "annoying." Gen X, millennials, and Gen Z, on the other hand, say they feel "entertained" by them. A lot is at stake. Advertisers are expected to spend $44 billion on creators in the US in 2026, per the Interactive Advertising Bureau. Here are four key stats from Morning Consult's survey on influencers. 1. Higher-income social media users are more likely to trust influencers More money, more loyalty — when it comes to trusting influencers. According to Morning Consult's survey, 61% of high earners — those making over $100,000 — trust influencer product recommendations. These high earners are also more likely to be politically swayed by creators and want to become influencers themselves. For those earning less than $100,000, that trust fell to about 50%. In part, that's because higher earners can better relate to some creators' lifestyles, industry insiders said. Amanda Acevedo, director of talent at G&B Digital Management, told Business Insider that the "general population online knows creators make good money for themselves." Meanwhile, creators and marketers alike are tempering the luxury overload — like hauls or gift unboxings — as financial realities their followers face ebb and flow. "When you are making more money, you don't view them as out of touch because you can relate to it a bit more — you have more spending power," said Natalie Barbu, founder of Rella and a former lifestyle influencer. Read more 2. Only 31% of baby boomers 'at least somewhat' trust influencers There's a generational divide in attitudes toward influencers. Baby boomers (born between 1946 and 1964) are more distrustful of influencers compared to millennials (1981 to 1996) and Gen Z (1997 to 2012). According to Morning Consult's survey, 31% of boomers said they trust influencer recommendations at least somewhat, compared with 62% of Gen Z and 64% of millennials. Still, they aren't immune to influencer marketing, according to Lucy Kruszynski, global head of brand at influencer marketing agency Buttermilk. "Brands need to think about how creators can build credibility through consistent content over time," she told Business Insider. Read more 3. 69% of US adults think paid promos should be disclosed — but only 25% think influencers are actually doing so consistently Knowing that you are watching or seeing an ad is very important to US consumers. Influencers who don't disclose such details risk losing the trust of their audiences. Morning Consult found that 69% of US adults want to see disclosures on sponsored influencer content . However, only 25% actually believe influencers are disclosing these partnerships consistently. That perception might not be reality. A survey of content creators conducted by SheSpeaks found that 14% of creators said they didn't always disclose brand ties. According to the same SheSpeaks data, 18% of surveyed creators said that a brand had explicitly requested that they not disclose a partnership. Read more 4. Influencers aren't just driving purchases — 26% of US adults say influencers have swayed their votes Influencer content has the power to move the political dial. According to Morning Consult, about one in four US adults said that an influencer's content had affected who they'd voted for in an election. Younger Americans were more likely to be politically swayed by influencer content, too. Morning Consult found that three in four Gen Z respondents said influencers had shaped their views on political or social issues. Influencer marketing is a "big player in this space now," said Nicole Dunger, a founding partner at the marketing firm People First, which works with candidates and advocacy groups on their creator strategies. title: I pivoted from an architecture career to work at Sweetgreen. I have no regrets.
summary: Sweetgreen manager Bahareh Ghazaei studied architecture but found her calling in restaurants, where she helps workers move up.
content: Bahareh Ghazaei trained as an architect but prefers working with people in restaurants. Courtesy of Sweetgreen Bahareh Ghazaei studied architecture before pursuing a career in restaurant management. She said working in restaurants gives her more tangible results than her past work as a designer. Ghazaei loves seeing staff at a new store grow: "When they all start to run, that's amazing to watch." This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bahareh Ghazaei, a general manager of restaurant chain Sweetgreen in Nashville. Ghazaei, 34, joined the company in 2021 after earning degrees in architecture and historic preservation. Business Insider verified her background. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. I was born and raised in Iran. I moved to the States around 2020, to LA. I have my bachelor's in architecture and my master's in historic preservation. It was a bit difficult to enter the architecture market and design with no prior experience in the US. I found a part-time server job at a local restaurant. It was my first job in the industry. Soon, I became the head server. I also trained a couple of people, and I loved it. When you're training, you leave someone with a skill that they can use for the rest of their lives, no matter what they do. I eventually got a job at Sweetgreen as a shift manager. In nine months, I became an assistant coach, meaning assistant manager. Then, after about a year, I became the head coach, or general manager . After being in the role for about two years, I became a head coach-restaurateur for the company. They are the top head coaches. They're nominated by regional general managers and interviewed by Sweetgreen's CEO and COO. Less than a year after that, I moved to Nashville to open up our new market. The calm in the storm I love the human interaction. I think that's one of the reasons I didn't pursue architecture seriously here. I would be sitting at a computer all day. When you work with people, that's a living example of what you did. That's mind-blowingly amazing for me. What I achieve on a daily basis in restaurants is more tangible for me than what I can get as a designer. When you're in a position of manager or a shift manager, you get to impact a lot of lives. You directly impact your team's lives , but you indirectly impact your customers because a happy team will then give you a happy customer. At my prior stores, I had almost all my dishwashers becoming shift managers. That's something that I'm super proud of. I think about how I'm leaving these people. As long as I leave them better than how I found them, my job is done. That could even mean firing them because they're wasting their time here. That could be developing them. Two of my shift leaders back home in LA are now general managers. As a manager, you sometimes have to be the calm in the storm — or sometimes be the storm in the calm, depending on the situation. What I mean is we try to be ready before our peak happens. One of the biggest problems at Sweetgreen is your oven going down. When your oven is down, or you're cooking with one oven, you really need to unlock the "yes" mentality in your team. Don't say, "I don't have salmon." Say, "I'm out of salmon right now, but I have this, this, and this." Or, "Here's what I can do right now." That's a very stressful situation. You say to your team, "Let them know our oven is down. We're working on it. Here is an ETA, and thank you for your patience." When they start to run We opened the Nashville store in June. The job is not done until I see this store on the right track for success over the next three months. Sweetgreen grades restaurants periodically and quarterly. Success means getting an A. I don't want to say I'm a perfectionist, but I strive for excellence. With a new store in a new market, it's challenging to teach everybody at the same time. I think about about a day care where you have everybody in the crawling-to-standing-up stage. You have to hold this one; you have to grab that one. But at the end of the day, when they all start to run, that's amazing to watch. When I think about my career , I always want to do more. There are careers in our support center or our corporate office. I can work toward becoming an area manager or a district manager. There are different paths. That's something that's kept me going.
