title: 'A golden age for builders': Here's what business leaders are thankful for this year
summary: Sam Altman said being a dad never gets old. Bill Ackman thanked the healthcare workers who have helped his daughter.
content: Sam Altman, Fei-Fei Li, and Bill Ackman posted about what they were thankful for this Thanksgiving. Getty Images CEOs, VCs, and other business leaders are feeling reflective. Sam Altman said being a dad never gets old. Bill Ackman thanked the healthcare workers who have helped his daughter. Fei-Fei Li and Brian Armstrong took different approaches to expressing their gratitude. It's not just your neighbor or family friend firing off a Thanksgiving post. Business leaders can't seem to resist either. Sam Altman took the opportunity to reflect on fatherhood. "I am thankful for a lot of things in life, but my family is the best thing that has ever happened to me," the OpenAI CEO wrote on X. "Most good things get a little less satisfying the 100th time you do them," Altman added. "A quiet evening hanging out with your kids, even doing very mundane stuff, is in the rare category of something repetitive just getting better and better." Altman is among a number of tech leaders, investors, and AI researchers who took to the internet to share what they're thankful for this year. Healthcare workers got a shoutout from billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who expressed appreciation for all the doctors, nurses, and others who helped his daughter with her recovery after she suffered a massive brain hemorrhage in February. She spent weeks in a coma and six months in the hospital. "Healthcare is a field, perhaps more so than any other, where people make a massive personal sacrifice of their lives, their time, their sleep, and their energy to help others," Ackman wrote on X. Investor and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, who has warned of a looming US debt crisis , emphasized the importance of connection amid turmoil in a post on LinkedIn. "I hope that we can keep in mind that despite all the challenges and conflicts in the world today, the most important thing is how we choose to be with each other," wrote Dalio. In a post on X, "Godmother of AI" Fei-Fei Li thanked the people in her life, including her students, colleagues, mentors, friends, and family, after noting that people often talk more about machines than each other. Li recently sold a startup she cofounded to AMD in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $8.2 billion. Meanwhile, AMD CEO Lisa Su shared a photo of herself with her Thanksgiving turkey on X, saying she was "very grateful" for the company's team, partners, and friends around the world. Every year, the Thanksgiving turkey is a new adventure! Wishing everyone a Happy Thanksgiving! Very grateful for our entire extended @AMD family and all of our partners and friends around the world. Hope you all enjoy a wonderful day with your loved ones! https://t.co/kJ9DcKvshX — Lisa Su (@LisaSu) November 26, 2026 Elon Musk , the world's richest man and CEO of Tesla, also marked Thanksgiving with a message of gratitude on X. "Super appreciate your support. Tesla wouldn't be where it is without our awesome customers," Musk wrote. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong leaned into the machine talk. "Today I'm thankful for technology, and living in a golden age for builders," he wrote, also on X. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger had technology, people, and religion on his mind. He said he was thankful for the teams he works with, the opportunity to build AI that serves humanity, his family, and his faith. Similarly, Apple executive chairman Tim Cook said he was grateful for family, friends, and the tech giant's employees and customers. He wasn't the only representative of the iPhone maker. Dinner with the Markkula's. Of course the pie was Apple. pic.twitter.com/uaI6Jy4CHv — Steve Wozniak (@stevewoz) November 26, 2026 Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak also showed his holiday spirit. He shared a photo on X of himself dining with Mike Markkula, an early Apple investor who later served as the company's CEO and chairman. "Of course the pie was Apple," Wozniak wrote. title: The vehicles that shaped Waymo's robotaxi fleet, from desert racers to luxury SUVs
summary: Waymo began as Google's secret Self-Driving Car project in 2008. Take a look at every vehicle that helped build its robotaxi fleet.
content: Waymo's robotaxis underwent multiple evolutions, including a concept for a Google-built car, before settling on electric SUVs. AP/Tony Avelar Waymo's operating robotaxi fleet is mainly made up of Jaguars and the Chinese-made Zeekrs. But did you know Waymo also designed a proprietary self-driving car with no steering wheel? Take a look at the different vehicle platforms Waymo explored before commercializing its service. Once upon a time, in Waymo's history , the Alphabet-backed robotaxi company designed its own autonomous car. Waymo, by now, is a 17-year-old project-turned-product that provides more than half a million fully autonomous rides a week and has started to expand beyond US roads. Its nearly two-decade legacy can be told through its pioneering figures, from Sebastian Thrun to Chris Urmson ; through its fierce rivalry with Cruise, Uber, and Tesla; through its evolution as a Google-backed business; or through its technology. Perhaps more vividly, though, the story of Waymo can be told through its cars. The Waymo robotaxi didn't immediately appear as the retrofitted Jaguar I-PACE most riders are familiar with today. Its earliest roots can be traced to a diesel-powered Volkswagen Touareg that competed in a desert race backed by the Department of Defense . As the company expands, Waymo has tapped companies abroad, including China's Zeekr and South Korea's Hyundai , to introduce newer vehicle platforms at lower costs. Take a look at all the cars that helped shape the robotaxi company. A 2004 Volkswagen Touareg retrofitted with a suite of sensors would get Google cofounder Larry Page's attention. Kim Kulish/Corbis via Getty Images In 2005, a Stanford University team led by Sebastian Thrun, pictured above, won the first-place, million-dollar prize in the DoD-backed Grand Challenge of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) for successfully building a car that can autonomously traverse 132 miles of Mojave Desert terrain. Volkswagen would provide Thrun's team with the base vehicle: a 2004 Volkswagen Touareg R5 TDI. The team would retrofit the car with five lasers, one camera, two radars, a GPS, and a six-processor Intel computer. The car was nicknamed Stanley, after the university. Stanley's victory caught the attention of Google cofounder Larry Page . Page would tap Thrun to lead what was then known as the Google Self-Driving Car project in 2008. A 2007 Chevrolet Tahoe showed that autonomous driving in urban environments was possible. David Paul Morris/Getty Images Two years after the Stanley victory, DARPA hosted another race. This time, the challenge required teams to navigate urban-like traffic rules and environments, including intersections, parking areas, and lane merging. A team from Carnegie Mellon University won first prize with a 2007 Chevrolet Tahoe named "Boss." The car was retrofitted with 13 lidars, 5 radars, and 2 cameras. Another key member of the Google Self-Driving Car Project emerged out of the race: Chris Urmson. Urmson acted as the project's chief technology officer before stepping into Thrun's role as the project leader in 2013. A modified 2008 Toyota Prius brought Google's self-driving dreams to real-world traffic environments. Karen Bleier/AFP via Getty Images The Toyota Prius made up Google's earliest real-world test fleet. The choice of the eco-friendly car could be traced to Anthony Levandowski, a technical lead in the Google project. In 2008, Levandowski, who by then had joined Google for its Streets project, and a team of Berkeley graduates built a self-driving Prius for a Discovery Channel series, "Prototype This!" The New Yorker reported. By 2009, Levandowski was brought in as a founding member of Google's autonomous driving project. The Prius would also become Google's first vehicle platform to receive an autonomous-vehicle testing license in Nevada. At the time, Nevada was the first state to create such a licensing regime for AVs. Google also had a brief taste for style with the Audi TT. Adrian Moser/Bloomberg via Getty Images Little's known about what was going through the minds of the folks at Google's self-driving project when they decided to include the Audi TT, a two-door luxury sports car, in its test fleet. The New York Times reported in 2010 that the project was using six Priuses and one Audi TT in its test fleet. A Waymo spokesperson told Business Insider that the TT was used as a support vehicle. The Lexus RX 450h was Google's first foray into self-driving SUVs. WASHINGTON, DC - APRIL 23: Googles Lexus RX 450H Self Driving Car is seen parked on Pennsylvania Ave. on April 23, 2014 in Washington, DC. Google has logged over 300,000 miles testing its self driving cars around the country. (Photo by Mark Wilson/Getty Images) Mark Wilson/Getty Images Urmson, in a 2012 blog post, said the hybrid Lexus was added to the test fleet to help the self-driving technology become familiar with "different environments and on different terrain." The New Yorker reported that the Lexus would be used for highway testing. The car also appeared to feature a sleeker and more compact sensor suite, Wired reported. Before the Tesla Cybercab, there was the Google Firefly. Scenes of daily life at Google X in Mountain View, California. A new Google self driving car is demonstrated for the media, elderly and legally blind test drivers at Google X in Mountain View, California. (Photo by Kim Kulish/Corbis via Getty Images) Kim Kulish/Corbis via Getty Images Google's Firefly was the company's vision for what self-driving vehicles should become: a car built for autonomy that removes the steering wheel, accelerator, and brake pedal. Press a button, and it will drive. The car was never meant to be commercialized, but more as a learning exercise, the company said. "By designing and building a truly self-driving vehicle from scratch, we were able to crack some of the earliest self-driving puzzles — where to place the sensors, how to integrate the computer, what controls passengers need in a car that drives itself," Waymo said in a blog post. The dome sensor on the roof of the Firefly would be the precursor to the now recognizable lidar hat on Waymo's current vehicle platforms. The company provided its first self-driving ride in a Firefly to a legally blind passenger, traversing some of Austin's roads. The 2017 Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid begins taking members of the public on autonomous rides. 07 May 2018, US, Mountain View: A self-driving car made by Google's sister company Waymo is on the road for a test drive. The car is a rebuilt minivan of the model Chrysler Pacifica by Fiat Chrysler. Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa (Photo by Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images) Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images In 2016, the Google Self-Driving Project announced a partnership with Fiat Chrysler Automobiles, which later became Stellantis, bringing Chrysler minivans to the robotaxi fleet. That same year, the project was spun out of Google and rebranded as Waymo. The car would see Waymo through its first early-rider program, which began in Phoenix in 2017, and through the first time the company opened its paid, fully driverless service to the public three years later. The Chrysler ran on Waymo's fourth-generation autonomous driving system. It had 6 lidars, 6 radars, and 19 cameras, a Waymo spokesperson said. Waymo retired the Chrysler in May 2023, giving the minivan a seven-year run. The Jaguar I-PACE scales Waymo's commercial robotaxi business. Two Waymo self-driving Jaguar robotaxies drive on Tower Bridge Road, on 11th September 2026, in London, England. Waymo are testing their vehicles around the capital using a driver at the wheel. Waymo say they're not yet offering commercial rides, but instead testing 24/7 to ensure their technology can safely handle all of London's road conditions. From September 3rd, self-driving cars have been available for hire in central London. (Photo by Richard Baker / In Pictures via Getty Images) Richard Baker/In Pictures via Getty Images The Chrysler helped jump-start the Waymo brand, but the Jaguar I-PACE, an all-electric SUV, would turn the company into a multi-city business. Waymo introduced the white Jaguars to the fleet in 2018. The cars quickly became a fixture of San Francisco roads even before Waymo began its paid service in the city in 2023. The car also introduced Waymo's fifth-generation driver, stacked with 29 cameras, 5 lidars, and 6 radars. Today, the Jaguar remains Waymo's main workhorse, making up the majority of the more than 4,000 robotaxis active across 15 metro regions in the US. The Chinese-made Zeekr CM1e introduces the cheaper, next-generation Waymo driver. Venice Beach, CA - May 27, 2026: Waymo's new autonomous vehicle, called the Ojai, drives in Venice Beach on Wednesday, May 27, 2026. The all-electric vehicle, equipped with the company's sixth-generation autonomous driving system, is expected to begin limited rides with select customers in Los Angeles, San Francisco and Phoenix in the coming weeks. (Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) The news is under embargo until May 28th at 8am. Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images With plans to go international and expand its robotaxi business, Waymo introduced a new vehicle platform that it said costs a fraction of what the Jaguar I-PACE costs. The vehicle is from Zeekr, a Chinese EV company, but Waymo rebranded the cars as Ojai. The car also came with the sixth-generation Waymo Driver, which includes a reduced sensor suite: 13 cameras, 4 lidars, and 6 radars. Waymo hasn't specified how much cheaper the Ojais are. The company has said that, in addition to lower vehicle costs, the Ojai is easier to clean and maintain. Business Insider reported during its ride test that the Ojai has more passenger room, more luggage space, and easier entry. The Hyundai Ioniq 5 will continue Waymo's expansion plans. LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 21: Waymo’s sixth-generation fully autonomous technology – the Waymo Driver – is outfitted on Hyundai’s all-electric IONIQ 5 SUV, which will be added to the Waymo One fleet over time, is on display during the Los Angeles Auto Show at the Los Angeles Convention Center on November 21, 2025 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Josh Lefkowitz/Getty Images) Josh Lefkowitz/Getty Images The Ioniq 5 , made by South Korea's Hyundai, is another extension of Waymo's ongoing expansion plans that's being tested on public roads. It'll come equipped with Waymo's sixth-generation driver. Both the Ojai and the Hyundai will make up Waymo's robotaxi fleet of the future, as the company eventually phases out the Jaguars. Semafor reported on Monday that Waymo has plans to increase its robotaxi fleet to 8,000 by the end of the year and to 20,000 by the end of 2027, citing people familiar with the matter. A Waymo spokesperson said it aims to roll out the Hyundai to the public sometime next year Read the original article on Business Insider

title: An exec wanted to better understand entrepreneurs, so he launched a candle company from his kitchen. Here's what he learned.
summary: The side-hustle experiment taught Ian Watson that making a product can be easier than navigating the paperwork required to sell it.
content: Ian Watson and his husband, Iain Cumming, started The Meltdown from their Palm Springs kitchen. Courtesy of Ian Watson Ian Watson started a side hustle to better understand entrepreneurs. He and his husband launched a cheekily branded candle business, selling scents like 'Sunday Panic' and 'FML.' Making the product was the easy part. Navigating permits and compliance took longer than anticipated. Ian Watson spends his workdays helping small businesses navigate payroll, benefits, and the other logistical realities of running a company. As Gusto 's chief customer officer, he wanted a more complete understanding of what it's actually like to start a business. It's a habit he's developed throughout his career in customer experience. While working at Qantas, he understood the frustration of delayed bags and disrupted trips as a traveler. At Airbnb, where he worked before Gusto, he became a host to better understand the anxiety of welcoming strangers into his home. Empathizing with entrepreneurs was a new challenge, Watson said, because he had never run a business himself. So he and his husband, Iain Cumming, started The Meltdown, a cheekily branded candle business selling highly relatable scents, from "Sunday Panic" and "Shady Pines" to "Gin & Regret" and "FML." They bought wax and fragrances, turned weekends into candle-testing sessions, and ran roughly 150 potential product names past friends and colleagues. The Palm Springs-based side hustle has already taught Watson two valuable lessons about entrepreneurship. 1. Making the product was easier than he expected Neither Watson nor his husband had made a candle before. They began with a basic kit designed to make six candles at home, then spent three months experimenting with scents, wax, branding, and packaging. "It was a lot of playing around and doing research to start with," Watson told Business Insider — both in terms of making the candles and developing the brand. The candle-making itself was "like mixology," he said. After experimenting with different scents, they gifted early versions to friends. Watson and Cumming started selling their candles at a local night market in Palm Springs. Courtesy of The Meltdown For the branding, they looked at the candle companies that resonated with them, those that didn't, and the gap they could fill. Much of the branding they encountered was rooted in health and wellness, Watson said, "but none of them are honest about what the real issue is — about why you're lighting a candle." Their answer was to build a brand around the messier realities their customers might actually be trying to escape. They went for "big and bold," he said, rather than discreet. View this post on Instagram A post shared by themeltdownps (@themeltdownps) So far, that strategy appears to be working. Once they mastered small-batch production, they used Claude to figure out how to scale while maintaining consistency. They launched at a weekly Palm Springs night market, where they found early customers and drew interest from local businesses looking to carry the candles wholesale. Next, they're focused on building a website to support online sales. "The actual making of a product is a lot easier than you think," Watson said. "If you've got an idea and something that you're passionate about, go do it." 2. Getting permission to sell the product was much harder Watson expected the business to be ready for its first market within about four weeks. Instead, it took closer to three months. Before selling a single candle, the couple had to register an LLC, secure seller's permits in California and Riverside County, shop for liability insurance, and pitch a farmers market review board for a spot. The Meltdown candles are hand-poured in Palm Springs. Courtesy of The Meltdown They also had to complete the required steps to use their business name. In California, that meant paying to publish it in a newspaper for four consecutive weeks while waiting to see whether anyone objected. "The fact that it takes a month before we can confirm that we can use that name — it's such an old, antiquated process," Watson said. "No one's looking at a newspaper anymore. That blew my mind." The experience gave Watson a sharper view of the pressures facing the entrepreneurs Gusto serves. The product may be the fun part, but the paperwork, compliance requirements, and costs can arrive long before the first sale. The couple's goal is to turn The Meltdown into a profitable business that can pay Cumming a salary. For now, their eight-year-old kid has one particularly fragrant bedroom: It doubles as their warehouse, with roughly 1,000 candles stacked on shelves. "It is the best-smelling eight-year-old bedroom in the world," Watson said. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I've flown to 14 countries with my cat. From airline rules to etiquette, here are 5 mistakes pet owners make when flying.
summary: Flying with a pet means following airline and country rules and avoiding habits that can derail your trip or annoy other passengers.
content: I travel full-time with my cat and have mastered the complexities of flying with her. Harrison Pierce I've spent the past five years traveling around the world with my cat, Isabelle. Through a lot of trial and error, we've almost perfected pet travel. I often see people let untrained pets out of carriers or misunderstand country entry rules. About five years ago, I sold almost everything I owned, bought a one-way ticket to Italy, and brought my four-year-old cat, Isabelle, along for the journey. Since then, we've flown thousands of miles on dozens of flights to 14 countries and counting across North America, South America, and Europe. Through trial and error — including mistakes that cost me thousands of dollars — we've turned pet travel into a science. Flying with a pet means following airline and country rules — and avoiding annoying habits that can inconvenience other passengers or derail a trip. Here are 5 things pet owners can get wrong at the airport. Letting your pet out of the carrier Isabelle fits in a pet carrier under the seat. Harrison Pierce Although you see pets on leashes all the time on social media, airline policies generally require pets to remain inside their carriers throughout the travel journey, including at the airport, in the lounge, on the plane, and upon landing. Service animals are subject to different rules. Still, I'm constantly seeing videos of cats asleep on airplane seats or perched on people's shoulders as they walk through the airport. It's cute and might make for viral content , but it can create a problem for everyone around you. Even if your pet is well-trained at home, an airport or airplane is an unfamiliar and stressful environment. Outside their carrier, a pet could escape, bother another traveler, trigger someone's allergies, or cause damage. I travel full-time with Isabelle, so the last thing I want is trouble with an airline or a pet escaping in a busy airport. I'm also aware that not every fellow passenger wants a cat crawling into their lap. Not preparing your pet for a long travel day The expandable cat carrier. Harrison Pierce When it's time to travel, I use a backpack-style carrier so I can keep my hands free. It's expandable, so when we're in a lounge, I can give Isabelle a little more room to move around. I pack her supplies in the carrier pockets and put the same blanket inside each time we fly so she has a familiar place to curl up. I find that familiar smells and routines help her settle into travel mode. I also make sure every opening on the carrier is fully secured before boarding. I've heard plenty of stories about owners not closing a carrier all the way and a pet slipping out at the airport or on the plane. I don't sedate Isabelle for flights. Sedation can pose health risks for pets during air travel, so I stick to natural calming treats. Waiting too long to add your pet to a flight Flights can only accommodate a small number of pets. Al Drago/Getty Images Most airlines limit the number of pets allowed in the cabin, so I book early and add Isabelle to my reservation as soon as I can. If you wait until close to departure or at check-in, the airline may already have reached its pet limit. Then, you may have to change flights and potentially pay a fee, depending on the fare you booked. Airlines can also have specific pet restrictions by route and destination. For example, most US airlines don't allow pets in the cabin on flights to or from Colombia. When I take Isabelle there, I fly a US airline from North Carolina to Miami and book a separate flight from Miami to Colombia on Colombian flag carrier Avianca. It adds another step to planning — and a connection that would solely be on the traveler to not miss — but it's much better than finding out your pet can't board after you've already booked a nonrefundable ticket. Not telling security you have a pet Security is the toughest part of the travel day. Al Drago/Getty Images Security is usually the most stressful part of the travel day, especially when I'm in a country where I don't speak the language. You generally need to remove your pet from the carrier and send the carrier through the X-ray machine. Then, you carry your pet through a metal detector before putting them back in the carrier. For Isabelle's first year of travel , I put her in a harness and leash before security in case she got scared and tried to run. We have a great routine now, and she usually sits calmly in my arms, so I no longer use a harness that could make her uncomfortable. I always tell security staff upfront that I have a pet. You can't go through a full-body scanner while holding an animal, and mentioning it early can save you the hassle of switching lanes. Not checking the entry rules and paperwork Isabelle has a passport. Harrison Pierce Before I book any flight, I check the destination's animal-import rules, including quarantine requirements, vaccinations, required tests, airline restrictions, and paperwork. Depending on the destination, that can mean getting a vet certificate shortly before travel and having it endorsed by a government agency before departure. When we arrive, officials review the paperwork and may charge an entry fee. Argentina, for example, didn't charge us anything, while other destinations have charged a nominal fee, often around $25. I avoid places that require long quarantines. I was considering a trip to Australia, but pets entering there from many countries may be subject to quarantine lasting 10 to 30 days. Since I usually stay in one place for only two or three months, that doesn't make sense for us. Isabelle travels everywhere with me. Harrison Pierce I've learned the importance of researching the required tests before booking flights the hard way. When I planned a trip to Peru, I didn't realize Isabelle needed a rabies titer test to enter from Europe, and I couldn't get it done in time. Instead, I had to make a last-minute detour to North Carolina to leave her with my parents for a couple of months. Luckily, I'd booked my original flight with miles, so it was refundable. Still, the detour added thousands of miles of flying, cost a couple hundred dollars in new tickets, and I couldn't cancel the nonrefundable, pet-friendly Airbnbs — which are often more expensive — that I no longer needed. The key is reviewing everything yourself. Not every vet regularly completes international pet health certificates, and a missing field, an incorrect date, or another small mistake can mean starting over, or being turned away at the border. title: I've traveled around Asia to countries like Japan and Thailand. They were nice, but the place I loved most surprised me.
summary: After traveling to several countries in Asia, my favorite place to visit is Taiwan. The cuisine, outdoor experiences, and locals made my trip great.
content: I've traveled across Asia, stopping at countries like Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam. Taiwan surprised me the most. Jenna DeLaurentis Taiwan is my favorite place I've visited in Asia, and the one that pleasantly surprised me most. The island has beautiful mountains and greenery, plus many amazing outdoor experiences. The delicious cuisine and friendly locals I met made my trip memorable, and I can't wait to return. Over the past few years, I've traveled to several parts of Asia , including Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. Every trip to the continent has been dynamic and exciting. The unfamiliar languages, lively night markets, rich cuisines, and futuristic cities keep drawing me back again and again. Although every place offers something unique, my visit to Taiwan took me by surprise the most. My husband and I had booked our trip with no expectations, but we left impressed by every aspect of the visit. The island's rugged landscapes are striking, making it a paradise for outdoor enthusiasts. The food, from juicy dumplings to made-to-order scallion pancakes, is mouthwatering, and the locals we encountered seemed approachable and friendly. After spending two weeks in Taiwan, I can safely say it's one of my favorite places in the whole region. Here's why I can't wait to plan a return trip. Taiwan is small and populous, but it never felt too crowded Even Taiwan's capital, Taipei, didn't feel too crowded during our visit. Jenna DeLaurentis Taiwan is a fairly small island — it's smaller than most US states — and is very densely populated, with over 20 million residents. It also has a bustling tourism industry. Despite these factors, Taiwan never seemed too crowded during my visit, whether I was at the beach or in its capital city, Taipei. I didn't notice severe overcrowding in touristy areas , and prices for hotels, tours, and transportation were lower than I experienced in other Asian nations for equivalent services. Fewer tourists meant I could enjoy popular attractions, like the Ximending Night Market and Taipei 101 skyscraper, without navigating through swarms of other visitors. For context, Taiwan expects to receive just over 9 million foreign tourists this year. In 2025, neighboring countries like Japan and Thailand received around 43 million and 33 million international visitors, respectively. Its landscapes and nature experiences felt out of this world Taiwan is a paradise for outdoor enthusiasts. Taroko Gorge is one of many beautiful spots we experienced. Jenna DeLaurentis Taiwan may look small on a map, but its landscapes feel incredibly diverse. Approximately 70% of its land area is covered by mountains featuring dozens and dozens of peaks. Its tallest mountain, Mount Yushan, is nearly 13,000 feet above sea level. At lower elevations, vibrant green rice fields stretch for miles in any direction, while more than 970 miles of stunning coastline frame the island's perimeter. We had some incredible nature experiences in Taiwan. Jenna DeLaurentis As someone who prefers nature-based travel over city trips, Taiwan ticked all the boxes. From scuba diving with turtles at Kenting National Park to cycling through dramatic scenery at Taroko Gorge, active adventures were around every corner. In terms of food, Taiwan is hard to beat I ate dan bing pancakes every day for breakfast in Taiwan Jenna DeLaurentis Prior to arriving in Taipei, I knew little about the local food. Taiwanese cuisine has gained greater recognition back in the US in recent years, thanks in part to the popularity of bubble tea and the success of the Taiwan-based restaurant chain Din Tai Fung. Even so, its popularity back home lags behind other Asian cuisines like Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese. I had no expectations, but I was blown away by the flavors I encountered during my trip. I started each morning with dan bing, a chewy egg crêpe stuffed with fillings like scallions and cheese. For lunch and dinner, I indulged in sesame noodles and soup dumplings , while my husband ordered his daily bowl of Taiwanese beef noodle soup. We had some incredible meals in Taipei. Jenna DeLaurentis For quick bites, Taiwan's 7-Eleven and FamilyMart locations rivaled the convenience stores' beloved locations in Japan. Each store was packed with ready-to-eat snacks, fun drinks, and quick heat-and-serve meals. Compared to what I've had in other Asian countries I've visited, Taiwanese food seemed to have the most recognizable flavors for my American palate. And though I've had incredible meals all over, Taiwanese cuisine surprised me the most. Friendly locals made my experience even better Locals I encountered seemed so friendly and approachable, which made my trip even better. Jenna DeLaurentis I've encountered friendly locals in every country I've visited in Asia, but the Taiwanese people seemed to take hospitality even further. Generally, I found locals here to be less reserved than those in other Asian countries I've visited. As a social, outgoing traveler, I appreciated the approachable nature many of them seemed to have. On one occasion, we arrived at a family-run hotel an hour prior to check-in. Rather than simply asking us to come back later, the owners treated us to a plate of tropical fruits and conversation until our room was ready. Another time, a train conductor chatted with us about our trip for a good 20 minutes, gifting us a "good luck coin" before disembarking at our next stop. Taiwanese locals frequently struck up conversations with my husband and me, whether we were sitting at a restaurant, riding the train, or swimming at the beach. The hospitality made us feel extremely welcome, and it was yet another reason we can't wait to visit Taiwan again. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: YouTube wants more paid users. Exclusive content like a new K-pop documentary could help.
summary: YouTube just released an exclusive film featuring Blackpink's Lisa, and it could signal a new playbook for differentiating itself from Netflix.
content: Lalisa Manobal (Lisa) at the premiere of "Always Lalisa," which is now exclusively available to YouTube Premium subscribers. Robin Marchant/Getty Images YouTube just released an exclusive documentary starring Blackpink's Lisa for its paid subscribers. Exclusives could be a useful marketing tool for YouTube as it aims to grow its Premium service. It could also help differentiate its paid offering as Netflix and others embrace creator content. YouTube wants to lure more users to its paid subscription offering, Premium. Will exclusive content help drive sign-ups? Last week, the company rolled out a Premium-only documentary featuring Lalisa Manobal, or Lisa, a solo artist and member of the K-pop group Blackpink. The Sony Music Vision film, "Always Lalisa," premiered in September at the Toronto International Film Festival and briefly showed up on Imax screens before landing on YouTube. YouTube hasn't publicly shared view counts for "Always Lalisa," but the trailer for the documentary drew 245 million views, suggesting it had wide appeal. Exclusive content isn't really part of YouTube's pitch for Premium, which focuses on ad-free videos, downloads, and background listening. But as competitors like Netflix begin to move onto its turf, adding content from YouTubers like Salish Matter and The Stokes Twins to its catalog alongside originals like "Stranger Things," the video app may need to respond in kind. Other streamers have successfully leveraged exclusives to score new sign-ups. In 2020, on the weekend that Disney Plus added the Broadway show "Hamilton" to its platform, it experienced a 7.4x spike in US sign-ups compared to the previous four weekends, according to estimates from the media analytics company Antenna. Peacock gained 2.8 million new subscribers during the first week of the 2024 Paris Olympics , which its owner NBC Universal broadcast exclusively in the US. YouTube could similarly drive some new Premium sign-ups if it can lock down exclusive content that matches the tastes of prospective subscribers using the data it already has on its more than 2 billion monthly active users, said Monica Khan, a former YouTube staffer who now runs an advisory firm for creators and brands called Creator Revolution. "Knowing my experience working at YouTube, everything is data-driven," Khan said. "YouTube should and will continue to selectively invest in exclusive creator programming when there is a compelling business case," she said. The company should use data to identify programming opportunities where there's "established fandom," she added. YouTube doesn't need to mess around with full-scale original productions like it did in the past, with mixed results. It produced shows like the karate drama "Cobra Kai" via its YouTube Red and YouTube Originals initiatives, but sunset its Originals program in 2022. YouTube Premium is an increasingly important revenue stream for the video app. While YouTube's ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter, it said its subscriptions business is growing faster than ads. The company in October said it had over 150 million YouTube Music and Premium subscribers, up from 125 million in March 2025. YouTube charges less than Netflix for its service. Its ad-free offering is $15.99 a month (or $8.99 for Premium Lite, a lower cost version that includes ads on YouTube Music), while Netflix starts at $19.99 a month.
